k: npsh npsha npshr cavitation impeller volute diffuser wear ring casing bep recirculation
x: A centrifugal pump adds energy to a liquid by spinning it. The impeller throws liquid outward, raising its velocity. The volute or diffuser then slows the liquid and turns that velocity into pressure. A pump makes head (metres of liquid), not pressure. The same pump lifts water and petrol to the same height, but the gauge reads differently because of the specific gravity. Pressure (bar) = Head (m) × SG ÷ 10.2

Part Job What to inspect Casing (volute or diffuser) Collects liquid, converts velocity to pressure Erosion at the cutwater, corrosion, gasket faces, cracks Impeller Gives energy to the liquid Vane tip erosion, cavitation pitting at the eye, blocked passages, balance Wear rings (casing and impeller) Control leakage from discharge back to suction Clearance against the new value, scoring, galling Shaft and sleeve Carries the impeller, protects the shaft under the seal Runout, wear under the seal, keyway damage, thread damage Bearing housing / frame Holds radial and thrust bearings, oil sump Bore

Closed : shrouds on both sides of the vanes. High efficiency, clean liquids. Uses wear rings. Semi-open : one shroud. Handles some solids. Efficiency depends on front clearance, set by axial adjustment (often 0.3–0.5 mm). Open : no shrouds. Slurries and stringy material. Single suction vs double suction : double suction halves NPSHr and balances axial thrust. Common in between-bearing pumps.

t: Centrifugal pump basics › NPSH and cavitation
x: NPSH (net positive suction head) is how far the suction pressure sits above the liquid's vapour pressure, in metres of liquid. NPSHa is what the system gives. NPSHr is what the pump needs, from the maker's curve (the point where head falls by 3%). NPSHa = (P_surface − P_vapour) × 10.2 ÷ SG + Z_static − H_friction P in bar absolute, Z positive if the liquid level is above the pump centreline. Keep NPSHa above NPSHr with a margin. A common rule is NPSHa ≥ NPSHr + 1 m, or a ratio of 1.1 to 1.3. High-energy pumps, hot water and hydrocarbons near boiling need more. Cavitation happens when pressure

Running far left of BEP (low flow) causes suction and discharge recirculation. Liquid turns back inside the impeller. It sounds like cavitation and damages the pressure side of the vanes and the shrouds. The fix is more flow: a minimum flow bypass, not a smaller suction valve.

Best: 80–110% of BEP flow. Allowable: roughly 70–120% of BEP for most process pumps (API 610 preferred range). Below minimum continuous flow: heating, recirculation, high vibration, seal and bearing damage. Far right of the curve: high NPSHr, cavitation, motor overload.

t: Centrifugal pump basics › Axial and radial thrust
x: Pressure acts unequally on the two sides of an impeller, making axial thrust toward suction. Makers balance it with balance holes and back wear rings, back vanes (pump-out vanes), opposed impellers in multistage pumps, or a balance drum or disc. Worn rings or blocked balance holes raise thrust and overload the thrust bearing. Radial thrust is lowest at BEP in a single volute and rises at low and high flow. Double volutes reduce it. High radial load bends the shaft and wears the seal faces and the rings.

Most centrifugal pumps can't pump air. Fill the casing and suction line before start. Vent at the casing high point until liquid flows without bubbles. Self-priming designs keep liquid in the casing to re-prime.

Permit closed, LOTO removed, guard fitted. Oil level correct, oiler filled, cooling water on. Seal flush and quench lines open, seal pot pressurised if fitted. Suction valve fully open, casing vented and primed. Discharge valve closed or cracked (centrifugal), per site procedure. Check rotation by bump if the motor was disconnected. Start, then open discharge slowly within 30 s to avoid running at shut-off. Check discharge pressure, amps, noise, seal leakage and bearing temperature. Take baseline vibration after 30 minutes. Never run dry or dead-headed. At shut-off all motor power turns into h

t: Pump curves & system curves › What the curve shows
x: A pump performance curve plots, against flow (Q): Head (H) : falls as flow rises. The point at zero flow is shut-off head. Efficiency (η) : rises to a peak at the best efficiency point (BEP), then falls. Power (P) : brake power, usually rises with flow for radial impellers. NPSHr : rises with flow, steeply at high flow. Curves are often drawn for several impeller diameters. The rated point is marked on the data sheet. Operating point Pump curve System curve Shut-off head Static head Flow Q → Head The pump runs where its curve meets the system curve. Throttling the discharge valve makes the sys

t: Pump curves & system curves › System curve
x: H_system = H_static + k × Q² Static head is the elevation difference plus the pressure difference between the two tanks. Friction rises with the square of flow. The pump settles where its curve crosses the system curve. Throttling discharge: adds friction, steeper system curve, less flow. Wastes energy but is simple. Clogged strainer or fouled exchanger: same effect as throttling. Higher destination tank pressure: raises static head, moves the whole curve up.

t: Pump curves & system curves › Affinity laws
x: For the same pump with a speed change (N), or a small impeller trim (D, up to about 10%): Q2 = Q1 × (N2/N1) H2 = H1 × (N2/N1)² P2 = P1 × (N2/N1)³ Cut speed by 20% and power drops to about 51%. That's why VFDs save so much energy on pumps with mainly friction head. With high static head the savings are smaller, because the pump must still overcome the static lift. NPSHr changes roughly with speed squared too.

t: Pump curves & system curves › Pumps in parallel
x: Heads stay the same, flows add at each head. The second pump adds much less than double the flow if the system curve is steep. Pumps must have similar shut-off heads. A weaker pump can be pushed back to shut-off and overheat. Each pump needs a check valve on the discharge.

t: Pump curves & system curves › Pumps in series
x: Flows stay the same, heads add. The second pump's casing must be rated for the combined pressure. Used for booster and transfer duties with high static head.

t: Pump curves & system curves › Specific speed
x: Ns = N × √Q ÷ H^0.75 (rpm, m³/s, m) Low Ns (below about 30 metric) means a narrow radial impeller, high head and low flow. High Ns means a mixed-flow or axial impeller, low head and high flow. Suction specific speed (Nss, using NPSHr) above about 11,000 US units (213 metric) warns of a narrow stable operating range.

t: Pump curves & system curves › Reading the field data
x: Read suction and discharge pressure gauges. Convert to head with SG. Differential head = (Pd − Ps) × 10.2 ÷ SG, plus the gauge height difference. Read flow from the flowmeter, or estimate from tank level change. Plot on the curve. Below the curve at the same flow means internal wear (rings, impeller) or wrong speed. Check amps against the power curve for SG and viscosity. Field rule. A pump making 10% less head than its curve at the same flow usually has worn wear rings, worn impeller or is turning slow. Check speed first, then open it up.

t: Pump types & API 610 codes › Vertical turbine pumps
x: Line shaft bearings: water-lubricated rubber or product-lubricated. Check each for wear at overhaul. Impeller lift set by the top adjusting nut. Lift = shaft stretch under thrust + running clearance. Too little and the impellers drag on the bowls. Follow the maker's lift. Column joints must be tight and square. Use thread compound on threaded columns. Check rotation before coupling. Reverse running unscrews threaded shafts. Non-reverse ratchet in the motor stops backspin on shutdown.

t: Pump types & API 610 codes › Multistage pumps
x: Several impellers in series on one shaft. Head adds stage by stage. Thrust balance: balance drum, balance disc, or opposed impellers (back-to-back). Assemble stages in the right order. Mark each diffuser and impeller on dismantling. Check total rotor float and the half-float position before fitting the thrust bearing. Balance line from the balance chamber to suction must be clear. A blocked line overloads the thrust bearing quickly.

t: Pump types & API 610 codes › Submersible pumps
x: Motor and pump in one sealed unit under the liquid. Common in sumps, wells and drainage. Check motor insulation (megger) and the oil chamber between seals at each service. Water in the oil means the lower seal is leaking. Check the cable entry. Never lift by the cable.

t: Pump overhaul procedure › Before you start
x: Permit, LOTO on the motor breaker, suction and discharge valves locked shut. Flush and seal lines isolated. Drain and vent the casing to a safe place. Check for zero pressure on the gauge. Gas test if the product is flammable or toxic. Take as-found readings: alignment, coupling gap, vibration history, seal leakage note. Get spares ready: seal, bearings, gaskets, O-rings, wear rings if due, lock washer and nut.

Remove coupling guard and spacer. Mark the hubs. Drain the bearing housing oil. Keep a sample for analysis. Disconnect seal flush and cooling lines. Cap the open ends. Fit the seal setting clips on the cartridge seal before loosening anything. Support the bearing frame with a sling or stand. Remove the casing bolts. Use jacking screws, never wedges between faces. Pull out the rotating assembly. Take it to a clean bench. Remove the impeller nut (usually left-hand thread on a clockwise pump, check). Remove the impeller with a puller if tight. Slide off the seal cartridge. Remove the coupling hub

t: Pump overhaul procedure › Inspect and measure
x: Item How Typical acceptance Shaft straightness Between centres or in V-blocks, dial at seal area, bearing seats and impeller fit ≤ 0.025 mm TIR (API), ≤ 0.05 mm general Bearing seats Micrometer, 2 positions × 2 planes Within the fit tolerance (e.g. k5) Housing bores Bore gauge Within H6/H7, no ovality above 0.01 mm Wear ring clearance Micrometer impeller ring OD, bore gauge casing ring ID Replace at 2× new clearance Impeller Visual, PT if cracked suspected No through-pitting, balance to G2.5 if repaired Impeller bore to shaft Measure Light interference or 0.01–0.03 mm clearance per OEM Keys Fi

Clean all parts. Blow out oil passages. Heat bearings on an induction heater to about 110 °C. Fit against the shoulder and hold until it grips. Fit angular contact pairs in the right arrangement (usually back-to-back, the "V" points outward on the outer rings' marks). Fit the lock washer and nut once the bearings cool. Tighten, then bend a tab. Fit the shaft into the housing, then the end covers. Check shaft end float with a dial: typical 0.05–0.10 mm for paired angular contact bearings, larger for ball/roller combos. Check shaft runout at the seal sleeve and the impeller fit, mounted in its o

Record at least: shaft runout (3 points), end float, ring clearances (old and new), bearing numbers fitted, seal serial number, impeller nut torque, final alignment readings, soft foot readings, coupling gap. Sign and date it. These numbers are the starting point for the next failure analysis. Tip. Photograph each part as removed. A failed seal face or bearing tells you why it failed. Keep them for the RCA, don't throw them in the scrap bin.

x: A positive displacement (PD) pump traps a fixed volume and pushes it out. Flow stays almost constant whatever the pressure. Pressure rises until the motor stalls or something breaks if the discharge is blocked. Always fit a relief valve on a PD pump discharge, set below the weakest component rating, and never start against a closed discharge valve.

t: Positive displacement pumps › Gear pump checks
x: End clearance (gear to side plate) controls slip more than tooth clearance. Typical total 0.05–0.13 mm. Measure with plastigage or by gasket thickness. Bushings worn oval allow gears to touch the casing. Look for a bright arc on the casing bore. Relief valve: test and set on the bench. Rotation: gear pumps are often direction-specific. Check the arrow.

t: Positive displacement pumps › Progressive cavity pumps
x: Never run dry. The stator burns in seconds. Stator swell from wrong elastomer causes high start torque and overload. Check pin joints or gear joints and their seals at each service. Flow drops as the stator wears. Measure output against new.

Air-operated double diaphragm (AODD) : no motor, can run dry, self-priming. Common for drainage and chemical transfer. Freezing at the air exhaust stops them; use a dry air supply. Check diaphragms, ball checks and seats. A torn diaphragm sends product out the air exhaust. Hydraulic diaphragm metering pumps : the plunger moves oil, oil flexes the diaphragm. Keep the oil topped and bled of air, or the stroke shortens.

t: Positive displacement pumps › Reciprocating plunger pumps
x: Used for high pressure: injection, glycol, chemical dosing, hydrotest pumps. Flow pulses with each stroke. Fit pulsation dampeners (nitrogen pre-charge typically 60–80% of operating pressure). Suction valves, discharge valves and plunger packing are the wear parts. Adjust packing to a slight weep where the design allows. Over-tight packing scores the plunger. Check crosshead and connecting rod bearings like a small engine. Suction needs good NPSHa. Acceleration head adds to the requirement, so keep suction lines short and large.

t: Positive displacement pumps › Metering pump calibration
x: Fill a calibration column (graduated cylinder on the suction). Close the tank supply so the pump draws from the column only. Time how much it draws in 60 s at the set stroke. Adjust stroke length or speed. Repeat at 3 settings and draw the calibration line.

k: troubleshooting fault finding no flow low head overload hot bearing seal leak noise vibration air lock
x: Work from the outside in. Check the system before opening the pump. Most pump problems are suction problems.

t: Pump troubleshooting › No flow or very low flow
x: Pump not primed, or air lock in the suction line (high spots). Suction valve closed, strainer blocked, foot valve stuck. Wrong rotation. Check by bumping the motor. 3-phase motors reverse when two phases are swapped. Speed too low (VFD setpoint, belt slip). Discharge head higher than shut-off (blocked line, closed downstream valve, wrong valve line-up). Impeller blocked or loose on the shaft (key sheared). Air leak at the suction: packing, flange gaskets, cracks. Air entrainment from a vortex at low tank level.

t: Pump troubleshooting › Flow or head lower than design
x: Worn wear rings or impeller. Compare with the curve at the same flow. Gas in the liquid, near boiling liquid. Higher viscosity than design. Impeller trimmed or wrong impeller fitted. Semi-open impeller front clearance too large.

Operating far right on the curve: low system resistance (a burst line, a bypass open). Higher SG or viscosity than design. Mechanical rubbing: wear rings, impeller to casing, bent shaft. Packing too tight. Electrical: low voltage, single phasing.

Clue Probable cause Gravel noise, unsteady gauges Cavitation (low NPSHa) or air entrainment Rumble at low flow Recirculation High 1X Impeller unbalance (damage, deposits), bent shaft High 1X/2X axial Misalignment, pipe strain Vane pass frequency high Impeller too close to cutwater, operating off BEP Bearing frequencies Bearing damage Changes when bolts are loosened Soft foot, base resonance, looseness

Too much grease, or oil level too high (churning). Oil level too low, oiler empty or on wrong side. Wrong oil viscosity, water in oil. Misalignment, too tight a fit, C3 bearing needed but CN fitted. High thrust from worn wear rings or blocked balance holes. Cooling water off on cooled housings.

Dry running at start-up or from vapour in the seal chamber. Vent properly. Flush orifice blocked, cooler fouled. Running off BEP: shaft deflection. Misalignment, pipe strain, bent shaft, worn bearings. Setting clips left in, or wrong setting length on a component seal. Elastomer not compatible with the product or flush. Solids in the seal chamber.

t: Pump troubleshooting › Pump loses prime after running
x: Suction air leak. Liquid level falls below the vortex limit. Gas coming out of the liquid (dissolved gas, temperature rise).

t: Pump troubleshooting › Good questions to ask the operator
x: When did it start? After maintenance, after a process change, slowly or suddenly? Is the flow and pressure the same as usual? Has the product changed (temperature, grade, density)? Is the spare pump doing the same? Any valves changed around the system?

k: mechanical seal cartridge component pusher bellows silicon carbide carbon tungsten elastomer viton epdm kalrez setting length face flatness light bands
x: A mechanical seal has two flat faces, one rotating with the shaft and one fixed in the gland. Springs or a bellows hold them together. A liquid film about 1 µm thick separates them. Faces are lapped flat to within 2–3 light bands (about 0.6–0.9 µm).

Primary ring (usually the flexibly mounted one, often carbon). Mating ring (seat, usually hard: SiC or tungsten carbide). Secondary seals : O-rings, wedges or bellows that seal the faces to shaft and gland. Springs : single coil spring, multiple small springs, or a metal bellows. Drive : set screws, drive pins or lugs. Gland plate with flush, quench, drain and vent ports. Sleeve (cartridge seals) with a locking collar.

Design Feature Use Pusher O-ring slides along the sleeve as faces wear General service up to ~175 °C. O-ring can hang up on deposits Non-pusher (metal bellows) Bellows flexes, no sliding seal Hot service up to ~400 °C with graphite seals, dirty or crystallising fluids Elastomer bellows Rubber bellows Water pumps, low cost Balanced Face area adjusted so closing force is lower Pressures above ~10 bar Unbalanced Full pressure on the face Low pressure, simple pumps Rotating spring Springs turn with the shaft Most common, simple Stationary spring Springs in the gland High speed, better tolerance to

Arrangement 1 : one seal per cartridge. Arrangement 2 : two seals, buffer fluid between at lower pressure than the seal chamber (unpressurised dual). Arrangement 3 : two seals, barrier fluid at higher pressure than the seal chamber (pressurised dual). Product cannot leak out.

Pair Use Carbon vs SiC The best general pair. Low friction, good heat removal Carbon vs tungsten carbide Good, slightly more heat SiC vs SiC Abrasives, slurries. Poor dry-running tolerance TC vs TC Slurries, high pressure Carbon vs ceramic (alumina) Water pumps, low cost. Ceramic cracks under thermal shock

Material Range Good for Avoid Nitrile (NBR) −30 to 100 °C Oils, water Ketones, ozone, strong acids Viton (FKM) −20 to 200 °C Hydrocarbons, many acids Hot water, steam, amines, ketones EPDM −40 to 150 °C Hot water, steam, glycols Any mineral oil or grease FFKM (Kalrez, Chemraz) up to ~300 °C Almost everything Cost PTFE −100 to 260 °C Chemicals Not elastic, needs spring energising

t: Mechanical seals › Installing a cartridge seal
x: Check shaft runout (≤ 0.05 mm), end float (≤ 0.10 mm) and radial play. Check seal chamber face runout and bore concentricity. Remove burrs and sharp edges on the shaft, keyways and threads. Tape them over. Lubricate the shaft and sleeve O-ring lightly with compatible lube. Slide on without twisting. Don't push on the faces. Bolt the gland evenly to the chamber with its gasket. Set impeller position first (axial adjust) on pumps that need it, then tighten the sleeve collar set screws. Remove the setting clips. Store them on the pump or in the job card. Connect flush, quench and vent. Vent the c

For a component seal, scribe a reference mark on the shaft at the seal chamber face, then measure the setting length from the drawing to set the rotating unit. Wrong setting length gives too much or too little spring load.

t: Seal flush plans (API 682) › Plan 53A filling and start-up
x: Fill the pot with clean barrier fluid (often a light oil or water/glycol) to the normal level. Vent the barrier circuit at the seal high point until fluid comes out free of air. Pressurise with N₂ to the set value above seal chamber pressure. Check the pumping ring is circulating: the return line to the pot warms after start. Record level and pressure each shift. A trend tells you which seal is leaking. Diagnosing with the pot. Plan 52: level up = process leaking in through the inner seal. Plan 53: level down with no visible leak = barrier leaking into the process through the inner seal.

k: gland packing stuffing box lantern ring braided ptfe graphite aramid leakage adjustment
x: Compression packing is rings of braided material squeezed in the stuffing box by a gland. It must leak a little. The leakage cools and lubricates the packing.

Packing Use PTFE-impregnated synthetic General water, chemicals Expanded PTFE with graphite (GFO) General pumps. Good heat transfer, low friction Aramid (Kevlar) Abrasive slurries. Hard on sleeves Flexible graphite die-formed rings Valves, high temperature steam Carbon fibre High temperature, high speed
Packing size = (Box bore − Shaft dia) ÷ 2 Number of rings = box depth ÷ packing size (allow for the lantern ring if fitted).

Wrap the packing around a mandrel the same size as the shaft. Never stretch it around. Cut with a sharp knife at 45° (skive cut) for pumps. Square cut is also used; follow the packing maker. Check each ring fits the shaft with no gap at the joint.

Remove all old packing with packing hooks. Don't scratch the sleeve. Clean the box. Check the sleeve: replace if grooved more than 0.25 mm. Check sleeve runout (≤ 0.08 mm) and box concentricity. Fit rings one at a time, seating each with a split tamping tool or the gland. Stagger the joints 90° (4 rings) or 120° (3 rings). Place the lantern ring in line with the flush port. Measure where it needs to be before you start. Fit the gland, nuts finger tight, then snug evenly. Don't crush.

Start with heavy leakage (a steady stream). Let it run 10–15 minutes. Tighten the gland nuts one flat (1/6 turn) at a time, evenly. Wait 10 minutes between adjustments. Aim for about 10–20 drops per minute per 25 mm of shaft dia, or the maker's figure. Gland should be cool enough to touch. Hot gland = over tight. Never run packing dry. No leakage means it's burning. The shaft sleeve scores and you get a big leak soon after.

Use die-formed graphite rings with braided anti-extrusion end rings for steam and hot service. Torque gland bolts to the packing maker's value, evenly. Live-loading (Belleville springs) keeps load on packing as it consolidates. Good for emissions (LDAR). Stroke the valve several times, then re-torque.

t: Rolling element bearings › Reading the number
x: Basic number : type + dimension series + bore code. For bore codes 04 and up, bore = code × 5 mm. Codes 00, 01, 02, 03 = 10, 12, 15, 17 mm. Bores below 10 mm and above 480 mm are written directly (e.g. 618/500). Example Meaning 6205 Deep groove ball, 2 (light) series, 25 mm bore 6310-2Z/C3 Medium series, 50 mm bore, metal shields both sides, C3 clearance 6205-2RS1 Rubber contact seals both sides (SKF). NSK uses DDU, FAG uses 2RSR NU 2216 ECP Cylindrical roller, no ribs on inner ring, 22 series, 80 mm bore, reinforced, polyamide cage 22220 E/C3 Spherical roller, 100 mm bore, C3 22220 EK Same wi

Class Meaning Use C2 Less than normal Precision, low noise CN (normal) Standard, not marked General C3 Greater than normal Electric motors, interference fits on both rings, warm shafts C4 Greater than C3 Hot running: kiln fans, dryer rolls, vibrating screens An interference fit expands the inner ring and reduces clearance. A hot shaft does the same. Not enough clearance makes the bearing preload itself and overheat.

Rule: the ring that rotates relative to the load direction needs an interference fit. On most pumps and motors the shaft turns and the load is fixed, so the inner ring is tight on the shaft and the outer ring is a slide fit in the housing. Application Shaft Housing Electric motors, pumps (ball bearings, normal load) j5 – k5 H7 (free end), J7 Medium/heavy roller loads m5 – m6 H7 Heavy load roller bearings, large n6 – p6 H7 / J7 Wheel hubs (rotating outer ring) g6 – h6 N7 – P7 Angular contact in pump thrust end k5 H6 / J6 (no outer ring rotation)

L10 (million revs) = (C / P)^p p = 3 for ball, 10/3 for roller L10h (hours) = L10 × 1,000,000 ÷ (60 × rpm) C is the dynamic load rating from the catalogue, P the equivalent load. Halving the load gives 8× the life for a ball bearing. In practice contamination and lubrication decide life more than load. API 610 asks for 25,000 h L10 at rated conditions (and 16,000 h at max loads).

t: Rolling element bearings › Reading bearing damage (ISO 15243)

Store flat in original packing, dry, 20 °C, away from vibration. Don't wash the preservative off until fitting (most modern preservatives are compatible with grease and oil). Sealed bearings have a shelf life of grease (often 3–5 years). FIFO stock rotation.

x: Work clean. Dirt kills bearings. Check shaft and housing dimensions before fitting. Apply force only to the ring being fitted. Never through the rolling elements. Never strike a bearing directly with a hammer. Don't heat above 120 °C (most bearings). Sealed and greased bearings: 80 °C max unless the maker says more. Never use an open flame.

Small bearings (bore up to about 50 mm) with light interference can be pressed or driven on cold. Use a fitting tool kit: an impact ring that spreads the force on the inner ring face and a sleeve. Use a press for larger sizes.

Induction heater : fast, clean, auto demagnetises. Use the temperature probe on the inner ring. Heat to about 80–90 °C above shaft temperature. For a 100 mm bore with 0.05 mm interference, ~ 50 °C rise is enough, but 110 °C gives sliding time. Slide on in one go, hold against the shoulder until it grips (it shrinks axially too). Hot plate or oven : OK for small batches. Oil baths are no longer recommended (fire, contamination). Expansion (mm) ≈ 0.000012 × bore (mm) × ΔT (°C)

t: Bearing mounting & removal › Tapered bore bearings
x: Spherical roller and some cylindrical roller bearings have a 1:12 taper. You set the fit by driving the bearing up the taper. As it goes up, the inner ring expands and the internal clearance reduces. Methods to judge drive-up: Clearance reduction : measure radial clearance with feelers over the unloaded rollers before and during drive-up. Stop at the reduction in the maker's table. Axial drive-up : measure axial distance travelled from the zero (start) position. Lock nut tightening angle : turn the nut a set angle from snug (small bearings). SKF Drive-up Method : hydraulic nut with a gauge to

t: Bearing mounting & removal › Adapter and withdrawal sleeves
x: Adapter sleeve (H series) : on plain shafts in plummer blocks. The nut pulls the bearing up the sleeve. Withdrawal sleeve (AH series) : pushed in under the bearing against a shaft shoulder. Removal nut pulls it out. Make sure sleeve thread is clean and oiled. Use a hook spanner, hydraulic nut for big sizes.

Pullers : grip the ring being removed. Use a back-plate puller behind the inner ring rather than pulling on the outer ring. Induction heater / aluminium heating ring for cylindrical roller inner rings with heavy fits. Oil injection : pump oil into a groove in the shaft seat to float the bearing off. Keep a nut on the shaft end so it can't fly off. Hydraulic nut : for withdrawal sleeves and big tapers. Cutting a bearing off with a torch is a last resort. It damages the shaft and creates hazards. Stored energy. A bearing coming off a taper or under oil pressure can release suddenly. Always fit a

t: Bearing mounting & removal › Plummer blocks (SNL, SD, SAF)
x: Locate one bearing (with locating rings) and leave the other free to slide for thermal expansion. Fill the housing with grease 25–40% of free space for normal speeds. Base surface must be flat; shim under the full base. Tighten cap bolts to the maker's torque. Caps and bases are matched pairs; don't swap.

k: journal bearing sleeve bearing tilting pad babbitt white metal crush clearance lift check thrust bearing kingsbury michell plastigage lead wire
x: Plain bearings carry the shaft on an oil film. With the right speed and oil, the shaft never touches the metal. They are used on large motors, turbines, compressors, big pumps and gearboxes.

Plain sleeve (cylindrical) : simple, prone to oil whirl at high speed. Lemon bore / elliptical : more stable at speed. Multi-lobe / pressure dam : better stability. Tilting pad journal : pads pivot to form their own wedge. Most stable. Standard on high-speed turbomachinery. Tilting pad thrust (Kingsbury / Michell) : pads on pivots or a levelling plate, carry axial load.

Tin-based babbitt (ASTM B23 grade 2 is common) on a steel shell. Soft enough to embed dirt and to wipe without scoring the shaft. Max operating metal temperature about 120–130 °C. Trip alarm on bearing RTDs is often around 115–120 °C.

Diametral clearance is typically 0.1–0.15% of journal diameter (1.0–1.5 mm per metre). High-speed machines often use 0.15–0.2%. Journal dia Typical diametral clearance 50 mm 0.05–0.08 mm 100 mm 0.10–0.15 mm 200 mm 0.20–0.30 mm 300 mm 0.30–0.45 mm

Micrometer and bore gauge : measure journal OD and bearing ID (shells bolted together at correct torque). Most accurate. Plastigage or lead wire : lay across the journal top, fit and torque the cap, remove and measure the squashed width or thickness. Lift check : dial on top of the shaft, lift with a bar or jack until it stops. Reading = top clearance. Quick check without opening. Feelers at the side of the bearing on a horizontal split (side clearance for elliptical bearings).

The bearing shell must be clamped in the housing so it can't move. Crush is how much the shell stands proud of the split line before the cap is tightened. Measure with lead wire or plastigage between shell back and cap. Typical crush 0.025–0.05 mm interference. Too little and the shell spins or frets. Too much and it distorts the bore.

t: Plain & tilting-pad bearings › Thrust bearing float
x: Mount a dial on the shaft end. Push the rotor fully one way with a bar (not on a seal or labyrinth). Zero the dial, push fully the other way. Reading = total float. Typical 0.25–0.40 mm on compressors and turbines, follow OEM. Adjust with shims behind the thrust pad carrier.

Finding Meaning Wiping (smeared babbitt) Oil film collapsed: low oil, start-up without lube, overload Fatigue cracks (crazed pattern) Cyclic load, vibration Scoring lines Dirt in the oil Embedded particles Dirt; light amount is OK, babbitt's job Bond failure (dull sound on tap, oil weeps at edge) Poor original bond or overheating. Check by UT or tap test Frosted or pitted (electrical) Shaft currents. Check grounding brush and insulation Black, hard areas Overheating, oil varnish Erosion near oil grooves Cavitation in oil film

Pressure lube systems: header pressure usually 1.0–1.7 bar g at the bearings. Oil supply temperature 40–50 °C, drain temperature rise about 10–25 °C. Check orifices in each bearing supply line are the correct size and clean. Ring-oiled bearings: check the oil ring turns and isn't distorted; level per mark.

x: Most bearing failures trace back to lubrication: wrong type, wrong amount, contamination or none at all. The five rights: right lubricant, right amount, right place, right time, right method .

Viscosity is the most important property. ISO VG number = kinematic viscosity in cSt (mm²/s) at 40 °C. VG 68 is 61.2–74.8 cSt. ISO VG Typical application 10–22 Spindles, light hydraulics, instrument air lubricators 32 Steam and gas turbines, centrifugal compressors, hydraulics 46 Hydraulics, turbines, some pump bearings 68 Most pump and fan oil-bath bearings, air compressors 100 Larger bearings, recip compressor crankcases, warm climates 150–220 Enclosed gearboxes (spur, helical), slow bearings 320 Heavy gearboxes, slow high load 460–680 Worm gears, very slow heavy gears 1000+ Open gears (ofte

R O (rust and oxidation inhibited) : turbines, compressors, circulating systems, most pumps. AW (antiwear) : hydraulics. Contains zinc (ZDDP) or ashless antiwear. EP (extreme pressure) : gearboxes. Sulphur-phosphorus additives. Avoid EP in systems with bronze worm wheels unless rated, and in turbines. Synthetic PAO : wide temperature range, long life, compatible with mineral oil. PAG (polyglycol) : worm gears, gas compressors. Not compatible with mineral oil and many paints and seals. Ester : fire-resistant hydraulics, biodegradable.

Grease = base oil (70–95%) + thickener + additives. The base oil does the lubricating. The thickener holds it like a sponge. NLGI grade Consistency Use 000–0 Fluid to very soft Centralised systems, gearboxes 1 Soft Cold climates, centralised systems 2 Normal (like peanut butter) Most rolling bearings 3 Firm Vertical shafts, high speed, warm Thickener Notes Lithium / lithium complex General purpose, most common. Complex: up to ~150 °C Polyurea Electric motors (sealed for life). Long life, high temp. Poor compatibility with others Calcium sulphonate complex Wet conditions, steel mills, marine Al

Mixing incompatible greases can make the mix soften and run out, or harden. Lithium complex is generally compatible with lithium and calcium complex; polyurea is often incompatible with lithium. When changing grease type, purge the old grease out fully and shorten the next interval.

Gp (grams) = 0.005 × D × B D = bearing outside diameter (mm), B = width (mm). This is the replenishment quantity for side-greased bearings (SKF formula). A grease gun stroke is typically 1–1.5 g; weigh a few strokes from your gun to find out. Initial fill: 30–50% of free space in the bearing, housing 30–50% for normal speed. Over-filling causes churning and heat.

Intervals depend on speed (n × dm), temperature, type and contamination. Halve the interval for every 15 °C above 70 °C. Vertical shafts: halve. Dirty or wet conditions: shorten more. Use the maker's chart or a calculator, and confirm with ultrasound or temperature trending.

Clean the nipple and the gun tip. Remove the drain plug if fitted. Pump the calculated amount slowly. With ultrasound, stop when the noise stops falling. Run the machine 20–30 minutes with the drain open to purge excess. Refit the drain plug. Record date and amount.

Horizontal shafts, ball bearings: oil level to the centre of the lowest ball (stopped). Higher speeds: lower level, or use an oil ring or flinger. Constant level oilers: mount on the side where rotation carries oil away from the oiler (against rotation), and set the height to the housing mark. Many have the arrow; follow it. Check housing vents. Pressurised housings push oil out of the seals.

Pure mist supplies fresh oil continuously to bearings and keeps housings under slight positive pressure, keeping out dirt and moisture. Common in refineries. Check the mist generator, header pressure, and reclassifier fittings at each bearing. A blocked fitting starves the bearing silently.

Store drums under cover, on their side with bungs at 3 and 9 o'clock. Label every container and grease gun with the product name. Colour-code by lubricant. Use filter carts and desiccant breathers on reservoirs. Use clean, dedicated transfer containers. Never open buckets.

t: Oil analysis › Taking a good sample
x: Take it from the same point every time, while the machine runs at normal temperature. Best point: a sample valve on the return line before the filter, or a live zone in the sump. Never from the drain at the bottom. Flush the valve and line first (5–10 times the dead volume). Use clean bottles. Fill to about 80%. Label right away: machine, date, hours, oil type. Send it within 24 hours.

With silicon: dirt Silicon (Si) Dirt and dust, or silicone antifoam additive Sodium (Na), Potassium (K) Coolant or seawater leak Zinc, Phosphorus, Calcium Additives. A change means wrong oil top-up

Three numbers for particles ≥ 4, ≥ 6 and ≥ 14 µm per mL. Each step up of 1 doubles the count. So 18/16/13 has twice the particles of 17/15/12. Cleaning oil by two codes can roughly double component life in hydraulics.

t: Oil analysis › Acting on a report
x: Read the trend, not just this sample. Caution: resample within 2 weeks and check the obvious (breather, seals, top-up records). Critical: inspect the machine, check vibration and temperature, plan an outage. Record what you found when you opened it. Feed it back to the lab or analyst.

k: shaft alignment laser alignment soft foot tolerance offset angularity thermal growth shims jack bolts bolt bound pipe strain
x: Misalignment loads bearings, seals and couplings. It shows up as high axial vibration, warm couplings, short bearing and seal life and wasted energy. Good alignment is the cheapest reliability improvement you can make.

Offset (parallel) : the distance between shaft centrelines, measured at the coupling centre. Expressed in mm. Angularity : the angle between centrelines. Expressed as a gap difference per 100 mm of diameter (mm/100 mm), or in mrad (1 mrad = 0.1 mm/100 mm). Both are measured in the vertical plane and the horizontal plane: four values in total. Stationary machine : the one you don't move (usually the pump or gearbox). Movable machine : usually the motor.

Safety : LOTO the driver, isolate the driven machine. Check both shafts can be turned. Prepare : clean the baseplate, feet and shims. Check bolts and holes. Have a set of precut stainless shims. Check run-out of the coupling hubs (≤ 0.05 mm) and that the shafts aren't bent. Rough align with a straight edge and feelers to within about 0.5 mm. Check soft foot on every foot and correct it (below). Check pipe strain on the stationary machine. Measure with laser or dials. Record as-found values. Correct vertical : add or remove shims under the movable machine's front and back feet. Correct horizont

Soft foot means one foot doesn't sit flat. Tightening its bolt twists the frame, distorts bearing bores and changes alignment. Tighten all foot bolts. Put a dial on one foot (or use the laser soft foot program). Loosen that bolt only. Read the rise. Retighten. Repeat for every foot. Any foot rising more than 0.05 mm needs correction. Type Check Fix Parallel (short foot) Feeler gauge shows the same gap all round the foot Add shim of that thickness Angled foot Gap varies across the foot Step shim or machine the foot / base Induced (from pipe or a bent foot) Reading changes with other bolts Remov

Mount dials on the stationary shaft or coupling in vertical and horizontal planes. Loosen the suction and discharge flange bolts. If the shaft moves more than 0.05 mm, the piping is forcing the machine. Fix supports or re-fit the spool. Never bend a pump to suit the pipe.

For short flexible couplings (values are at the coupling centre): Speed (rpm) Offset excellent Offset acceptable Angular excellent Angular acceptable 600 0.13 0.23 0.09 /100 0.13 /100 750–1000 0.07 0.13 0.06 /100 0.10 /100 1500 0.06 0.09 0.05 /100 0.07 /100 3000 0.03 0.06 0.03 /100 0.04 /100 6000 0.02 0.03 0.02 /100 0.03 /100 Spacer couplings are judged by angle across each flex element: a common limit is 0.5 mm per metre of spacer length (0.5 mrad) for 3000 rpm.

With rim-face or laser data you calculate corrections at the front feet and back feet. The laser does it for you. By hand: Foot correction = Offset + (Angle × Distance from coupling centre to foot) Use angle as a slope (mm per mm). Watch the sign: positive means the movable machine is high and you remove shims.

t: Shaft alignment › Bolt bound and base bound
x: Bolt bound : the motor can't move far enough sideways because the bolts hit the holes. Move the stationary machine slightly, or open the holes on the movable one (with engineering approval). Base bound : the motor needs to go lower but there are no shims left. Raise the stationary machine or machine the base.

Machines grow as they warm. A hot pump centreline rises; a motor grows a little. Set the cold alignment so the shafts come into line hot. ΔL (mm) = α × L (mm) × ΔT (°C) steel α = 0.0000117 Example: pump centreline 450 mm above the base, casing support temperature rises 60 °C: ΔL = 0.0000117 × 450 × 60 = 0.32 mm. Set the pump 0.32 mm low compared with the motor cold (or the motor 0.32 mm high), minus the motor's own growth. Makers often give cold offsets on the alignment drawing. Hot alignment checks (with probes, or Dodd bars, or a laser hot check right after shutdown) confirm them.
Vertical pumps with a rigid motor stand are checked for squareness of the motor mounting face and concentricity (rabbet fit). Shim between motor and stand only if the design allows.

Turn both shafts together in the direction of rotation for readings. Don't use a coupling spider as a lever for turning. Use precut stainless shims, never more than 4 per foot. Mark the thickness. Leave the movable machine with some shim under every foot (0.5–1 mm) for future correction. Recheck alignment after the first 24–48 h of running on new installations.

k: dial indicator rim and face reverse dial reverse indicator bracket sag tir graphical plotting calculation
x: Lasers are faster, but every supervisor should be able to align with dial indicators. You need two dials, a solid bracket, a calculator, and patience.

t: Dial indicator alignment methods › Rules for dial readings
x: Zero the dial at 12 o'clock. Read at 3, 6 and 9. Valid readings follow the rule: 12 + 6 = 3 + 9 (within 0.02 mm). If not, the bracket is loose, the dial sticks, or there's axial float. Rim readings are TIR. Actual centreline offset = reading ÷ 2. Plunger in (positive) means the surface is coming toward the dial. Turn both shafts together so the dial stays on the same spot.

t: Dial indicator alignment methods › Bracket sag
x: The bracket and dial bend under gravity. At 6 o'clock the dial reads more negative than it should. Clamp the bracket on a rigid pipe of similar diameter, with the same span. Zero the dial at 12 o'clock. Rotate to 6 o'clock. Read. This is the sag (always negative, for example −0.08). Correct the bottom rim reading: subtract the sag (−0.20 measured − (−0.08) = −0.12 true).

t: Dial indicator alignment methods › Rim and face method
x: A rim dial measures offset. A face dial measures angle. Both mounted from the stationary shaft onto the movable hub. Vertical offset at the dial plane = (bottom rim reading, sag corrected) ÷ 2. Vertical angle = bottom face reading ÷ diameter of the face sweep (in mm/mm). Front foot correction = offset + angle × (distance from dial plane to front foot). Back foot correction = offset + angle × (distance to back foot). Good for large couplings and where one shaft can't be turned (rotate only the stationary one with the dial). Face readings are spoiled by axial float. Push the shafts the same way

t: Dial indicator alignment methods › Reverse dial method
x: Two rim dials. One on the stationary shaft reading the movable hub (S→M), one on the movable shaft reading the stationary hub (M→S). The distance between dial planes is the "span". Slope = (M_rim/2 + S_rim/2) ÷ span Then project to each foot. Sign conventions differ between textbooks, so the easiest way by hand is graphical plotting: Draw the machine to scale on graph paper: dial planes, feet, distances. Draw the stationary centreline as a horizontal line. Plot half of each corrected bottom reading at its dial plane, above or below the line by sign. Draw a straight line through the two points:

t: Dial indicator alignment methods › Worked example (vertical, reverse dial)
x: Convention used here: dials zeroed at 12 o'clock, plunger pushed in reads positive, bottom readings already corrected for sag. With that convention, a positive bottom reading means the shaft being measured sits low compared with the shaft carrying the dial, by half the reading. Dial A is on the stationary shaft, reading the movable (motor) hub. Bottom reading +0.40 mm. So the motor centreline is 0.20 mm low at plane A. Dial B is on the motor shaft, reading the stationary hub, 200 mm away toward the pump. Bottom reading +0.10 mm. The pump is 0.05 mm low compared with the motor, so the motor is

t: Dial indicator alignment methods › Horizontal moves
x: Set two dials on the motor feet (front and back) on the side, touching from a fixed point. Zero them. Move with jack bolts while watching the dials until they show the calculated move. Tighten bolts and recheck: the motor often moves while tightening.

x: Quantity Unit Best for Displacement µm pk-pk (mils) Low speed, shaft movement in sleeve bearings (proximity probes) Velocity mm/s RMS (in/s pk) Overall machine condition 10–1000 Hz. The standard for most plant machines Acceleration g (m/s²) High frequency: bearing defects, gear mesh Conversions: in/s pk × 25.4 ÷ 1.414 = mm/s RMS. 0.3 in/s pk ≈ 5.4 mm/s RMS.

On every bearing housing: horizontal (H), vertical (V) and axial (A). As close to the bearing load zone as possible, on solid metal, not on covers or fins. Same spot every time. Mark it or fit a stud. Magnet mounting is good to about 2 kHz (flat rare-earth magnet higher). Hand-held probes only for quick checks. Machine at normal load and temperature.

Machine Foundation A/B B/C C/D Group 2: 15–300 kW Rigid 1.4 2.8 4.5 Group 2 Flexible 2.3 4.5 7.1 Group 1: 300 kW–50 MW Rigid 2.3 4.5 7.1 Group 1 Flexible 3.5 7.1 11.0 mm/s RMS, 10–1000 Hz on bearing housings. A = new. B = unrestricted long-term. C = limited period, plan repair. D = damage likely. A foundation is "rigid" if the machine's lowest natural frequency on it is at least 25% above running speed. API 610 pumps: overall limit for new pumps on test is typically 3.0 mm/s RMS (bearing housing), within the preferred operating range.

t: Vibration analysis › Trending is more useful than limits
x: A machine running steadily at 4 mm/s may be fine. One that went from 1.5 to 3 mm/s in a month has a problem developing. A doubling from baseline is a common alert level.
The FFT spectrum splits the signal into frequencies. Everything is related to running speed: 1X = running speed. A 2960 rpm motor: 1X = 49.3 Hz.

Fault Spectrum Other clues Static unbalance High 1X radial, low harmonics H and V phase differ ~90°; phase same on both bearings Couple unbalance High 1X radial Phase ~180° between the two bearings Overhung rotor unbalance 1X radial and high 1X axial Axial phase in-phase Angular misalignment High 1X axial, often 2X, 3X Axial phase ~180° across coupling Parallel misalignment High 2X radial, 1X Radial phase ~180° across coupling Bent shaft 1X axial dominant, some 2X Axial phase 180° end to end of the same shaft Mechanical looseness (structural) 1X high in one direction Phase differs between foot

BPFO (ball pass outer race): about 0.4 × number of balls × rpm. BPFI (inner race): about 0.6 × number of balls × rpm, with 1X sidebands. BSF (ball spin), FTF (cage, about 0.4X). Software calculates them from the bearing number. Inner race defects show sidebands at 1X because the defect rotates in and out of the load zone. Stages of bearing failure: 1) ultrasonic only (stress waves, 20 kHz), 2) envelope/demod peaks at defect frequencies, 3) defect frequencies visible in the velocity spectrum with harmonics, 4) noise floor rises, 1X rises, discrete peaks disappear into haystack. Replace in stage

Phase compares the timing of vibration at two points, using a tachometer reference or two channels. It tells unbalance from misalignment from bent shaft when the spectra look the same. Take phase in H, V and A at each bearing.

With the machine stopped, hit the structure with a soft-faced mallet and capture the ring-down spectrum. Peaks show natural frequencies. A natural frequency within ±20% of 1X or another forcing frequency is a resonance risk.
Watch the live reading and cut the power. If the vibration drops instantly, the cause is electrical. If it coasts down with speed, it's mechanical.

k: balancing field balancing single plane two plane trial weight influence coefficient iso 1940 iso 21940 g6.3 g2.5 vector polar plot

x: Static : heavy spot on one side. The rotor turns to rest heavy side down. Fixed in one plane. Couple : two equal heavy spots 180° apart on opposite ends. Statically balanced but wobbles. Needs two planes. Dynamic : a mix of both. The general case on wide rotors. Needs two planes. Rule of thumb: rotors with length/diameter below about 0.5 (fans, pulleys, narrow impellers) can often be done in one plane.

t: Balancing › Balance quality grades (ISO 21940-11, was ISO 1940)
x: Grade Typical rotor G40 Car wheels, crankshafts of slow engines G16 Agricultural machinery, crushers G6.3 Fans, pump impellers, flywheels, general machinery G2.5 Turbines, compressors, motor rotors, high speed pumps, machine tool drives G1 Grinders, tape recorders, precision spindles Permissible residual unbalance U (g·mm) = 9549 × G × M ÷ n M = rotor mass (kg), n = rpm, G = grade. Divide U by the correction radius (mm) to get grams. Split between planes as the rotor geometry requires (half each for a symmetrical rotor). Example: 120 kg fan impeller at 1480 rpm, G6.3: U = 9549 × 6.3 × 120 ÷ 14

Confirm it's unbalance: dominant 1X radial, phase steady, H/V phase ~90° apart. Clean the rotor. Deposits cause most fan unbalance. Check for looseness, cracked blades, bearing wear, eccentric pulleys, resonance. Balancing can't fix those. Check the rotor isn't rubbing.

Mount the sensor radially on the bearing nearest the plane. Mount the tacho on a reflective mark on the shaft. Run 0 (original) : record 1X amplitude and phase (e.g. 8.0 mm/s at 60°). Choose a trial weight that changes the reading by at least 30% (or gives a force of about 10% of rotor weight). Fit it at a known angle and radius. Record its mass and position. Run 1 : record new amplitude and phase (e.g. 5.0 mm/s at 140°). The instrument (or vector math) works out the effect of the trial weight: T = Run1 − Run0. Correction weight = trial weight × (|O| ÷ |T|), placed at angle shifted by the angl

Measure angles in the same direction every time. Most instruments say "against rotation" or "with rotation". Mark the rotor with angles before starting. If the phase moved the wrong way after the first correction, check the convention.

Used when there is no tacho. Take the original amplitude, then run with the trial weight at 0°, 120° and 240°. Draw circles with radii equal to each reading on a polar plot; their intersection gives the correction. Slower but needs only an amplitude meter.

Two sensors (one per bearing), two trial weights (one per plane, one at a time). Runs: original, trial in plane 1, trial in plane 2. The instrument solves the influence coefficients and gives correction weights for both planes. Keep the same sensor positions throughout.

Weld-on weights: weld only with the welding earth clamped on the rotor, never through bearings. Use a qualified welder and approved procedure. Bolt-on and clip-on weights: check they can't come loose at speed. Use thread locker. Grinding or drilling to remove metal: check with engineering for strength. Record final weights, positions and readings on the job card. Thrown weights kill. Stay out of the plane of rotation during runs. Guard fitted for every run.

k: condition monitoring thermography infrared ultrasound airborne ultrasonic motor current signature analysis mcsa performance monitoring route pdm pf curve

x: A fault starts at a point (P) where it can first be detected, and grows to functional failure (F). Different methods see it at different times: Ultrasound and oil analysis (earliest) Vibration analysis Thermography Audible noise Hot to touch Failure Inspection intervals should be shorter than half the P-F interval, so you catch the fault at least once before it fails.

Finds hot bearings, misaligned couplings, blocked coolers, refractory failures, steam trap failures, electrical hot joints. Emissivity matters. Shiny metal reads low. Use electrical tape or paint as a reference spot. Compare similar items under similar load (phase A vs B vs C, pump A vs pump B). A ΔT of 10 °C between like items is worth investigating; above 40 °C is serious for electrical joints. Electrical scans need at least 40% load and qualified people with switchgear access.

t: Condition monitoring › Airborne and contact ultrasound
x: Hears friction and impacts above human hearing (20–100 kHz, usually 30–40 kHz). Uses: bearing condition and greasing, compressed air and gas leaks, steam traps, valve passing, electrical arcing and corona. Greasing with ultrasound: listen while greasing, stop when the dB reading drops to its lowest and starts to rise again. An increase of 8 dB above baseline: lack of lubrication. 12–16 dB: early failure. 35 dB+: approaching failure.

t: Condition monitoring › Motor current signature analysis (MCSA)
x: Measures current in one phase with a clamp. Shows broken rotor bars (sidebands at pole pass frequency around line frequency), eccentricity, and some load problems. Done from the MCC without going near the motor.

Pumps: head, flow, power: compare with the curve to see internal wear. Compressors: efficiency, discharge temperature, ratio, valve temperatures on recips. Heat exchangers: approach temperatures, ΔP, fouling factor. Fans: ΔP and amps.

t: Condition monitoring › Setting up a route
x: Rank the equipment by criticality (safety, production, cost of failure, redundancy). Choose methods per machine (vibration, oil, thermography, ultrasound). Set intervals: monthly for critical rotating, quarterly for less critical; continuous online monitoring for the most critical turbomachinery. Mark measurement points. Take baselines after overhaul. Set alarm levels (absolute and trend-based). Write a short report for each alarm with a clear action and a due date. Close the loop: what was found when it was opened, and was the call right?
