DBSE (distance between shaft ends) is set on the drawing. Spacer couplings give room to remove a seal or bearing housing without moving the motor. Check DBSE at installation and after changing a motor. Too short and the disc pack or gear teeth are axially loaded.

Keyed with clearance fit : set screw over the key. Use thread locker. Keyed interference fit : heat the hub (induction or oven) to 100–150 °C. Typical interference 0.0005 × shaft dia. Keyless hydraulic fit (taper) : pushed up a taper with oil injection. Advance set by drawing. Used on big compressors. Taper-lock bushes : tighten screws evenly to torque. Common on pulleys and small couplings. Keys must fit the keyway sides snugly with clearance on top. A tight-top key pushes the hub off centre. Hub face flush with shaft end unless drawn otherwise.

Elastomer elements: cracks, hardening, swelling, dust under the guard (wearing). Gear couplings: tooth wear (pointed or stepped teeth), lubricant condition, seals. Grid: grid wear at the contact points, grease condition. Replace grid and grease together. Disc packs: cracked laminations, fretting, bolt looseness. Check with a torch and mirror. Bolts: correct grade, torque, same weight (matched sets on balanced couplings). Guard fitted, no rubbing.

Misalignment beyond the coupling's rating. No or wrong grease (gear, grid). Wrong DBSE or axial pre-load. Shock overloads, torsional vibration (engines, compressors). Wrong bolts, loose bolts. A coupling's misalignment rating is not the alignment tolerance. It can survive 0.5 mm offset, but your bearings and seal can't. Always align to the machine tolerance.

k: gearbox gear helical spur bevel worm planetary backlash tooth contact prussian blue pitting scuffing breather oil level shim tapered roller endplay

x: Type Notes Spur Straight teeth, parallel shafts. Simple, noisy at speed. No axial thrust Helical Angled teeth. Quieter, stronger, creates axial thrust. Most industrial reducers Double helical / herringbone Thrust cancels. High power turbine gears Straight / spiral bevel Shafts at 90°. Spiral bevel quieter. Set by shims for contact pattern Worm and wheel High ratio in one stage, low efficiency at high ratios, can be self-locking. Bronze wheel Planetary (epicyclic) Compact, high torque. Sun, planets, ring and carrier

Backlash is the free play between meshing teeth. It allows for oil film, heat and tolerances. Lock one gear (pinion usually). Mount a dial indicator on a tooth of the other gear, perpendicular to the tooth, at the pitch circle. Rock the gear back and forth. Read total movement. Repeat at 3–4 positions around the gear. Typical industrial backlash: about 0.03–0.06 × module (mm) for helical gears, more for large or hot gears. Use the maker's figure.

Clean teeth with solvent. Paint 3–4 teeth of the pinion thinly with Prussian blue or marking compound. Rotate the gears through mesh under light braking. Read the pattern transferred to the mating gear. Good: contact over 80% or more of face width and centred about the pitch line. Contact at one end: misalignment, shafts not parallel, housing distortion, bearing wear. Contact at tips or roots only: wrong centre distance. For bevel gears, adjust the pinion position (shims behind the pinion bearing cage) and gear position to centre the pattern.

Tapered roller bearings are set with a small endplay (e.g. 0.05–0.10 mm) or preload, using shims under the end cap. Measure endplay with a dial on the shaft end while pushing and pulling. Hot running increases preload in some arrangements. Follow the maker.

Use the right ISO VG (often 150–320 for industrial helical, 460–680 for worm) and type (EP mineral, PAO synthetic, PAG for worms only if specified). Fill to the sight glass or dipstick mark with the gearbox stopped. Change interval: 2,500–5,000 h mineral, 10,000 h+ synthetic, or by oil analysis. Clean breathers. Fit desiccant breathers in wet or dusty areas. Oil temperature under about 90 °C mineral, 100 °C synthetic.

Damage Looks like Cause Running-in polish Shiny smooth flanks Normal Micropitting (grey staining) Matt grey frosted areas Thin oil film, high load, rough surfaces Macropitting Craters near pitch line Surface fatigue, overload Spalling Large flakes out Advanced pitting, case crushing Scuffing / scoring Radial streaks from tip to root, welded material Oil film failure, wrong oil, high speed and load Abrasive wear Scratches, step at end of contact Dirty oil Plastic flow Rolled-over tips, ridges Overload on soft gears Tooth breakage (fatigue) Beach marks on fracture face, at root Overload, misalig

Shaft centre distance and parallelism (housing bore check). All bearings, seals, shims recorded and replaced. Gear runout on the shaft. Housing split face flatness, sealant (anaerobic) on metal-to-metal joints. Clean all magnetic plugs. Look at what's on them before cleaning.

k: v belt wedge belt spz spa spb timing belt synchronous belt tension deflection pulley alignment sheave groove gauge roller chain sprocket elongation

x: Section Top width (mm) Notes Z / SPZ 10 / 9.7 Small drives A / SPA 13 / 12.7 B / SPB 17 / 16.3 Most common in plants C / SPC 22 / 22 Large drives 3V, 5V, 8V 9.5, 16, 25.4 American narrow sections SP sections are wedge (narrow) belts carrying more power than classical belts of the same width. Never mix sections or brands on one drive.

Use a laser pulley tool or a straight edge across both pulley faces. Check parallel offset and angular (both vertical and horizontal) misalignment. Maximum: about 0.5° angular for V-belts, 0.25° for timing belts. Offset ≤ 1 mm per 100 mm of centre distance (V-belts). Pulleys with different face widths: measure from the groove centre, not the face.

Measure the span length (between the contact points). Deflection = 16 mm per 1,000 mm of span (1/64 inch per inch). Press the centre of the span with a tension gauge until it deflects that amount. Compare the force with the belt maker's table for the section and small pulley size. Run 30 min to 24 h, then re-tension (new belts stretch most in the first hours). Sonic tension meters measure the belt's natural frequency, which is more accurate. Enter belt mass and span. Signs of too low tension: squeal at start, slip, glazed sides, heat. Too high: bearing overload, short belt and bearing life.

t: Belt & chain drives › Inspecting belts and pulleys
x: Cracks on the underside, glazing, swelling (oil), uneven wear. Belt riding low in the groove: worn groove or worn belt. Use a groove gauge. Shiny groove bottom = bottoming out. Replace all belts in a set together, with matched lengths. Never roll belts on with a screwdriver. Move the motor in.

Profiles: HTD (5M, 8M, 14M), GT, T5, T10, XL, L, H. Need correct tension but less than V-belts. Too loose: ratcheting (jumping teeth). Pulleys must have flanges on at least one pulley. Never crimp or bend tight: the tensile cords break.

ISO / ANSI sizes: pitch in eighths of an inch for ANSI (40 = 1/2", 50 = 5/8", 60 = 3/4", 80 = 1"). ISO 08B = 1/2", 10B = 5/8", 12B = 3/4", 16B = 1" (British standard dimensions). Sag: about 2–3% of centre distance on horizontal drives. Elongation : measure over a number of pitches under light tension. Replace at 1.5% elongation for general drives (2% for slow drives; 1% for high speed or timing). Replace sprockets when teeth are hooked or pointed. Fit a new chain with new sprockets on worn drives. Lubricate: drip, bath or brush with a good chain oil. Dry chains wear 10× faster. Connecting link

k: electric motor induction motor iec nema frame bearing drive end non drive end insulation megger shaft current vfd grounding brush cooling fan ip rating soft foot
x: Electrical isolation, terminal work and testing belong to the electricians. The mechanical team usually handles bearings, couplings, alignment, mounting, cooling and lubrication.

Power (kW or HP), voltage, current, frequency, speed (rpm at full load), power factor, efficiency class (IE2, IE3, IE4). Frame size (IEC: shaft height in mm, e.g. 160M; NEMA: e.g. 254T). Bearing numbers DE (drive end) and NDE (non-drive end), grease type and interval. Insulation class (F = 155 °C, H = 180 °C), IP rating, duty type (S1 continuous). Ex marking for hazardous areas: don't modify these motors without certified repair.
Synchronous speed = 120 × f ÷ poles At 50 Hz: 2-pole 3000 rpm, 4-pole 1500, 6-pole 1000, 8-pole 750. Actual speed is lower by the slip (1–5%), e.g. 2960 rpm.

Usually deep groove ball bearings, C3 clearance. Large motors: cylindrical roller at the DE (for belt loads) and ball at the NDE (locating). Roller bearing DE on a direct coupled motor with little radial load can skid and fail. Check the bearing suits the drive type. Grease: often polyurea or lithium complex NLGI 2–3. Don't mix. Follow the nameplate interval. Locked bearing on the NDE, floating on the DE (or as the maker specifies).

t: Electric motors (mechanical side) › Shaft currents and VFDs
x: Variable frequency drives create common-mode voltage that discharges through the bearings, causing fluting. Signs: frosted raceways, washboard pattern, early failures on VFD motors. Fit insulated bearings (ceramic-coated outer ring) at the NDE, or hybrid ceramic balls. Fit a shaft grounding ring or brush at the DE. Use proper VFD cable with symmetrical earth and 360° gland earthing.

TEFC motors (totally enclosed fan cooled): keep fins clean. Every 10 °C over rating halves insulation life. Check the fan cowl isn't blocked or dented onto the fan. Large motors: check air filters, heat exchangers (air-to-air or air-to-water), and space heaters (on when stopped to prevent condensation).

t: Electric motors (mechanical side) › Insulation resistance (for information)
x: The electrician meggers the winding before starting a motor that has been idle or wet. A common minimum is 1 MΩ plus 1 MΩ per kV of rating; many sites use 100 MΩ as healthy for LV. Polarisation index (PI = 10-min/1-min reading) above 2 is good.

Soft foot and alignment, as for pumps. Shaft runout and end float (sleeve bearing motors have a magnetic centre marked on the shaft; set the coupling so the rotor runs at magnetic centre within the float limits). Feet and base bolts tight. Drain holes at the bottom of the frame open (condensation). Rotation: uncouple and bump-test with the electrician before coupling to direction-sensitive machines.

t: Electric motors (mechanical side) › Storage of spare motors
x: Dry, heated store. Space heaters energised if fitted. Rotate the shaft several turns every month to redistribute grease and prevent false brinelling. Lock the rotor for transport on roller bearing motors (transport lock). Megger before installing.

k: hydraulic pump cylinder valve directional control relief valve accumulator filter fluid cleanliness iso 4406 hose fitting jic orfs bsp symbols troubleshooting

t: Hydraulic systems › Parts of a system
x: Component Job Reservoir Stores oil, lets air and dirt settle, cools. Size about 3× pump flow per minute Pump (gear, vane, piston) Makes flow. Pressure comes from resistance Relief valve Limits maximum pressure Directional control valve Sends flow to the actuators. Solenoid, manual, pilot or proportional Flow control valve Sets speed Check valve, pilot-operated check One-way flow, load holding Counterbalance valve Controls overrunning loads (cranes, lifts) Cylinder Linear motion. Force = pressure × area Motor Rotary motion Accumulator Stores energy, damps pulses, emergency power Filters Suction

About 70–80% of hydraulic failures come from contaminated fluid. Servo and proportional valves need ISO 4406 16/14/11 or cleaner; general systems 18/16/13; piston pumps 17/15/12. Filter new oil when filling. New oil is often dirtier than the system needs. Use desiccant breathers. Cap every open hose and port immediately. Change filter elements on ΔP indicator, not only by hours.

Bladder, piston or diaphragm type, pre-charged with dry nitrogen only . Never oxygen or air. Pre-charge typically 0.9 × minimum system pressure (energy storage) or 0.6–0.8 × working pressure (pulsation). Check pre-charge with the oil side at zero pressure, using a charging kit. Stored energy. Before working on any hydraulic circuit: stop the pump, lower or block loads, dump accumulators to tank, and check gauges read zero. A pin-hole leak at 200 bar can inject oil through skin. That is a surgical emergency.

Hoses: SAE 100R2 / EN 853 2SN (two wire braid) common for medium pressure; 4SP/4SH spiral for high pressure. Minimum bend radius from the hose table. No twist after fitting (watch the lay line). Common threads: BSPP (parallel, with bonded seal), BSPT, NPT, JIC 37° flare, ORFS (O-ring face seal, best for leaks), metric DIN 24° cone (DKO). Never mix JIC and 45° SAE flare. They look similar but leak. Replace hoses at the age limit (often 5–6 years) or on damage.

Symptom Check No pressure Pump not turning, coupling broken, relief valve stuck open, oil level low, wrong valve position Slow actuator Pump wear (check case drain flow on piston pumps), internal leakage, flow control setting, relief setting low Noisy pump Cavitation (blocked suction strainer, cold oil, high suction lift), aeration (air leak on suction, low oil level) Oil overheating Relief valve dumping continuously, cooler fouled, internal leakage, wrong viscosity Cylinder drifts Piston seal leak, valve spool leakage, pilot check leaking Erratic motion Air in system, sticking valve, dirt Cyl

k: compressed air pneumatic frl filter regulator lubricator dryer refrigerated desiccant iso 8573 dew point leak cylinder solenoid valve actuator

x: Aftercooler removes most water right after the compressor. Receiver stores air and lets water settle. Drain daily or fit auto drains. Dryers : refrigerated (dew point +3 °C, general use), desiccant (−40 °C or −70 °C, instrument air), membrane (small users). Filters : general (5 µm), coalescing (0.01 µm, removes oil aerosols), activated carbon (oil vapour).

t: Compressed air & pneumatics › Air quality ISO 8573-1
x: Written as particles:water:oil, e.g. 1.4.1 for oil-free instrument air, 2.2.2 for instrument air with desiccant dryer. Instrument air typically needs a pressure dew point at least 10 °C below the lowest ambient temperature.

t: Compressed air & pneumatics › FRL unit at the machine
x: Filter : drains water, catches dirt. Check and drain bowl. Regulator : sets working pressure. Set the lowest pressure that does the job. Lubricator : only where components need it. Most modern valves and cylinders are pre-lubed for life; adding oil then washes the grease out and you must keep oiling.

Single acting (spring return) and double acting cylinders. Rotary actuators (rack and pinion, scotch yoke) on quarter-turn valves. Spring return is fail-safe. Cushioning screws at the cylinder ends set the end-of-stroke deceleration.

Ports/positions: a 5/2 valve has 5 ports and 2 positions (standard for double-acting cylinders). A 3/2 valve has 3 ports and 2 positions (single acting cylinders, pilot signals). Port numbers (ISO 5599): 1 supply, 2 and 4 outlets, 3 and 5 exhaust, 12/14 pilots.

Leaks are typically 20–30% of compressor output on an unmanaged site. A 3 mm hole at 7 bar wastes roughly 10 L/s, around 3 kW of compressor power, all year. Survey with an ultrasonic detector during production, and again at shutdown (you can hear leaks on a quiet weekend). Tag each leak with a number and log it. Fix fittings, hoses, quick couplers, FRL drains, and cylinder rod seals. Re-survey every 6 months.

Never use compressed air to clean clothes or skin. Air injection kills. Use blow guns limited to 2 bar at the nozzle (OSHA 30 psi) with chip guard. Whip restraints on hoses above 12 mm or where a coupling could fail. Vent to zero before breaking any connection.

k: reciprocating compressor recip valve plate poppet piston rod runout rod drop rider band wear band packing crosshead crankshaft deflection bumping clearance unloader

x: Frame : crankcase, crankshaft, main bearings, connecting rods. Crosshead : converts the rod's rocking motion to straight motion. Runs on guides. Distance piece : space between frame and cylinder, separating oil from gas. Single or double compartment. Piston rod packing : rings in a packing case seal gas along the rod. Cylinder : liner, piston, piston rings, rider (wear) bands. Valves : suction and discharge, plate, ring, poppet or channel type. Unloaders : finger unloaders, plug unloaders or clearance pockets for capacity control.

Valves cause around 40% of recip compressor unplanned stops. Suction and discharge valves look alike but install opposite ways. Most designs physically prevent wrong fitting; always check the arrow or the "S"/"D" marking. Check plates and rings for cracks, chips, wear. Springs for broken coils and set height. Lap seats flat. Replace plates rather than reusing cracked ones. Use new gaskets on valve seats. Tighten valve cover bolts in a cross pattern to torque. Leaky valves show as high valve cover temperature (thermography or contact probes). A hot suction valve cover is a classic sign.

Item Method Typical guide (use OEM) Main bearing clearance Lift check / plastigage 0.001 × journal dia Connecting rod big end Feeler, plastigage 0.001 × dia Crankshaft end float Dial on shaft end 0.15–0.40 mm Crankshaft web deflection Deflection gauge between webs at 4–5 positions Usually 0.0001 × stroke Crosshead to guide Feeler on top (crosshead resting on bottom) 0.0008–0.001 × crosshead dia Piston end clearance (bumping) Lead wire through valve port, bar the piston over Head end and crank end per drawing, e.g. 1.5–3 mm Piston ring end gap Feeler with ring in the liner Per material and dia

Mount a dial on the frame near the packing, touching the rod top (vertical) and side (horizontal). Bar the machine over a full stroke. Typical limit: vertical and horizontal ≤ 0.0015 mm per mm of stroke (API 618: about 0.0006 in per in of stroke). Large vertical runout: worn crosshead shoes, worn rider bands, misaligned cylinder. Large horizontal runout: piston not square on the rod, crosshead guide misalignment, bent rod.
As rider bands wear, the piston sinks and the rod drops at the packing. A proximity probe under the rod at the packing case measures it online. Set an alarm at about 50–60% of allowable band wear.

Packing rings: radial cut and tangential cut pairs, with a backup ring. Fit in the right order and direction (the side marked to the pressure). Vent and purge connections must be clear. Rising vent flow means packing wear. Check the rod finish where it runs in the packing: polish out scratches, hard-coated rods must not be ground.

Lube oil pump on, pressure normal. Cylinder lubricator primed and feeding (check each point). Cooling water flowing through jackets. Bar over at least 2 full turns by hand or barring device. Feel for liquid lock or rubbing. Drain knockout drums and suction scrubbers. Start unloaded. Load in steps once temperatures are stable. Check valve cover temperatures, rod packing temperature and vibration. Liquid in the cylinder breaks rods and heads. Check scrubbers, levels and drains every shift on wet gas service.

k: centrifugal compressor surge anti surge stonewall choke dry gas seal seal oil lube oil console rotor float thrust bearing labyrinth balance piston slow roll api 617

x: At low flow the compressor can't keep up its pressure ratio. Flow reverses through the machine, then recovers, many times a second. You hear and feel heavy banging, and see pressure and flow swinging. Surge damages thrust bearings, seals, labyrinths and impellers. The surge line on the map marks the minimum stable flow at each speed. The anti-surge controller opens a recycle valve to keep flow a margin (often 10%) to the right of the surge line. Never block or manually close the anti-surge valve while running. Stonewall (choke) : at very high flow the gas reaches sonic speed in the impeller an

Two rings: a rotating ring with spiral grooves and a stationary ring. The grooves pump gas between the faces and lift them apart by about 3–5 µm. No contact when running. Primary seal gas : clean, dry, filtered process gas or N₂, supplied above process pressure. Separation gas (N₂ or air) at the barrier seal keeps bearing oil out of the gas seal. Separation gas must be on before the lube oil starts and stay on after it stops. Oil reaching the seal faces destroys them. Watch primary vent flow trends. Rising vent flow = primary seal wear. Seal gas must be above dew point (heaters) and filtered t

Main and auxiliary oil pumps. Auxiliary starts on low pressure. Twin coolers and twin filters with changeover valve. Fill and vent the standby side before switching. Rundown tank or accumulator to supply oil during coast-down after a power failure. Oil temperature to bearings 40–50 °C. Test auxiliary pump auto-start regularly.

t: Centrifugal compressors › Rotor checks at overhaul
x: Total rotor float (thrust bearings removed): records the axial position of impellers relative to diffusers. Thrust bearing float and position. Set the rotor so impellers line up with diffuser channels. Journal bearing clearances, pad thickness. Labyrinth clearances (diametral), by feeler or lead. Rotor runout at journals, probe areas and impeller eyes. Probe area runout (mechanical + electrical) for proximity probes: typical limit 25% of allowable vibration or 6 µm. Impeller inspection: fouling, erosion, cracks (dye penetrant or MT on blades and eye). Balance piston and its labyrinth: worn bal

t: Centrifugal compressors › Slow roll and barring
x: After shutdown, a hot rotor bends if left still (top cools faster). Keep it turning on the turning gear until the casing cools. Before start-up, slow roll to check runout at the probes is within normal (shows bow).

k: screw compressor rotary screw oil flooded oil free separator element minimum pressure valve thermostatic valve intake valve load unload vsd air receiver

x: Oil injected into the rotors seals, cools and lubricates. Discharge temperature 70–100 °C. Separator element strips oil from the air. Replace when ΔP reaches the limit (often 0.7–1 bar) or by hours. Minimum pressure valve keeps pressure in the separator for oil circulation. Thermostatic valve sends oil through or around the cooler to keep discharge above the dew point. Scavenge line returns oil from the separator. A blocked orifice gives high oil carry-over.

Rotors don't touch. Timing gears keep them in phase. Two stages with an intercooler. Rotor coatings wear: performance falls. Element exchange at OEM hours. Check intercooler and aftercooler, drains and condensate traps.

Load/unload : inlet valve opens or closes between pressure set points. Unloaded power is still 25–35% of full load. Modulation : throttles the inlet. Inefficient at low flow. VSD : varies speed. Best efficiency for varying demand. Use one VSD trim machine with fixed-speed base load machines. Use a master controller to sequence them.

Interval Task Daily Check oil level, discharge temp, pressure, alarms. Drain receiver and traps Weekly Check air filter indicator, cooler cleanliness, condensate drains 2,000 h Air filter, oil filter 4,000–8,000 h Oil change (depends on oil type), separator element Yearly Safety valve test, minimum pressure valve, thermostatic valve, hoses 24,000–40,000 h Bearings / element overhaul

Fault Causes High discharge temperature trip Low oil, cooler blocked (dust on fins), thermostatic valve stuck, high ambient, oil filter blocked High oil carry-over Separator element failed, scavenge line blocked, oil level too high, low pressure operation Won't build pressure Inlet valve stuck, leak, belt slip, demand higher than capacity Safety valve lifting Pressure switch fault, valve faulty, blocked separator element Water in oil (milky) Running too cool, oversized compressor running unloaded
Pressure vessels: need inspection per local law, safety valve set at or below design pressure. Drain daily. Fit zero-loss drains instead of timer drains. Check for corrosion at the drain area.

k: steam turbine overspeed trip test governor woodward trip throttle valve gland seal condensing back pressure extraction warm up barring blade nozzle

x: Back pressure : exhausts to a lower pressure steam header. Common for pump and fan drives. Condensing : exhausts to a vacuum condenser. Most power from the steam. Extraction : steam taken out at an intermediate stage for process. Impulse (steam expands in nozzles, pushes blades) vs reaction (expands in both fixed and moving blades). Most small turbines are impulse (Curtis or Rateau stages).

Overspeed trip : mechanical bolt or electronic. Typical trip at 110% of maximum continuous speed (MCS). API 611/612. Trip and throttle valve (T T) : closes on a trip. Must be exercised regularly to prove it moves freely. Other trips: low lube oil pressure, high vibration, high axial displacement, high exhaust pressure, low vacuum.

Done with operations and a procedure. Uncoupled (solo) for the first test after overhaul if required. Confirm speed indication is accurate (calibrated tachometer). Raise speed slowly with the governor override or test device. Record the trip speed. Repeat to confirm (often 3 times within ±1%). Adjust the mechanical trip spring if out of range, per OEM. Never bypass or gag the trip to run the turbine.

Lube oil on, temperature at least 25–30 °C. Open all casing and steam line drains. Warm the inlet line to the T T valve. Start the gland seal steam (condensing) and then pull vacuum. Crack the T T valve, roll the rotor slowly (often 300–500 rpm) and hold for the warm-up time. Listen for rubs. Watch vibration and casing expansion. Increase speed through criticals quickly to the governor range. Close drains when dry steam appears. Water induction from undrained lines can bend rotors, crack blades and break thrust bearings. Drain properly and never rush a cold start.

Small turbines use a mechanical-hydraulic governor (e.g. Woodward TG, PG) or an electronic one. Check governor oil level and grade, linkage free play, and droop setting (often 4%). Hunting speed: linkage wear, wrong compensation needle setting, sticky governor valve.

Journal and thrust bearing clearances, thrust float. Rotor runout, blade tip and shroud condition, cracks (dye penetrant on blade roots and disc). Erosion of last-stage blades (wet steam) and nozzles. Labyrinth and carbon ring gland seals: replace carbon rings, set clearances. Governor valve and T T valve: stem straightness, seat condition, packing. Casing horizontal joint: clean, check flatness, use correct compound sparingly, torque bolts hot or by stretch where specified. Steam strainer at the inlet: clean and check for missing pieces.

k: gas turbine combustion hot gas path borescope compressor wash inlet filter major overhaul eoh fired hours
x: Gas turbines are usually maintained under an OEM long-term service agreement, but the site mechanical team supports every outage and does the routine work.

Inlet : filter house (pulse-jet or static), silencer, anti-icing. Compressor : axial, many stages. Inlet guide vanes (IGVs) control airflow. Combustion : can-annular or annular combustors, fuel nozzles, igniters, flame detectors. Turbine : hot gas path (HGP) stages, nozzles and buckets with cooling holes. Exhaust : diffuser, to stack or heat recovery steam generator (HRSG).

Based on equivalent operating hours (EOH) or starts (whichever comes first), because starts and trips cause thermal fatigue. Combustion inspection: every 8,000–12,000 EOH (varies a lot by model). Hot gas path inspection: every 24,000 EOH. Major overhaul: every 48,000 EOH.

Inlet filter ΔP monitoring and change-out. Compressor washing : online (running) and offline (crank wash). Restores power lost to fouling, often 2–5%. Borescope inspections of compressor, combustors and HGP between outages. Lube oil system, filters, coolers, vent fans. Fuel gas filters and coalescers. Enclosure ventilation, fire and gas detection, CO₂ or water-mist systems (with lockout before entry). Enclosure entry. Gas turbine enclosures have CO₂ fire suppression. Lock out the system and follow the entry permit before going in.

k: fan centrifugal fan axial fan blower roots blower id fan fd fan damper inlet cone impeller fan laws belt driven

x: Type Notes Centrifugal, backward curved Efficient, non-overloading power curve. Clean air, FD fans Centrifugal, radial blade Dirty, dusty air. Self-cleaning, rugged Centrifugal, forward curved Low pressure HVAC. Overloads at high flow Axial, vane axial High flow, low pressure. Cooling towers, tunnels, air coolers Positive displacement (Roots blower) Fixed volume. Aeration, pneumatic conveying. Needs relief valve
Same as pumps: flow ∝ speed, pressure ∝ speed², power ∝ speed³. Air density changes pressure and power: a cold start on a hot-gas fan (ID fan) draws much more power. Start with the damper closed.

Impeller: build-up, erosion of blade leading edges, cracks at welds (blade to back plate). MT or PT on welds. Inlet cone to impeller overlap and radial gap: even all round. Typical gap 0.5–1% of impeller diameter. Shaft seals at the casing. Bearings: plummer blocks, oil level or grease. Locating and floating bearings set correctly. Dampers and inlet vanes: free movement, linkage wear, actuator stroke, full open matches indicator. Flexible connections: tears. Foundation bolts, grout, base. Belt drives: alignment, tension, guards.

t: Fans & blowers › Axial fans (air coolers, cooling towers)
x: Blade pitch angle: set all blades the same with a protractor, at the same radius. Typical tolerance ±0.5°. Tip clearance to the fan ring: commonly 0.5% of diameter or the maker's figure, min. 6–10 mm. Hub bolts torqued, blade clamps tight. Vibration switches tested. Gearbox (right-angle) oil level and breather; drive shaft and couplings.

Timing gears keep lobes apart. Check gear backlash and lobe clearances with feelers. Don't run above rated pressure: relief valve on discharge. Oil both gear end and drive end sumps; levels differ. Check silencers and inlet filters.

k: agitator mixer top entry side entry impeller steady bearing gearbox shaft runout seal vessel
x: Top-entry : motor and gearbox on a vessel nozzle, long overhung shaft, impellers (pitched blade, hydrofoil, Rushton turbine). Side-entry : large storage tanks. Seal replacement often possible with the tank full using a shut-off device. Bottom-entry : mixing at low level. Seal in contact with the product.

Shaft runout at the seal: typically ≤ 0.1 mm for mechanical seals; check after impeller fitting. Shaft runout at the bottom end: check against OEM (long shafts amplify small errors at the gearbox flange). Steady bearing (bottom bush) wear if fitted. Impeller blade angle and bolting. Use thread locker and lock wires. Gearbox oil and dry-well (no oil leak into the vessel). Mounting flange level and bolt torque.

Don't run with the impeller near the liquid surface or above it (unsteady loads) unless designed for it. Check rotation: some impellers pump down and must turn one way. Agitator seals often use a dual seal with barrier pot (Plan 53A) for reactors. Vessel entry. An agitator is a major hazard during confined space entry. Lock out the motor electrically and, if possible, mechanically restrain or uncouple the shaft.

k: conveyor belt tracking idler pulley take up splice vulcanised scraper skirt pull wire lagging

x: Drive pulley (lagged), tail pulley, bend and snub pulleys. Carrying idlers (troughed), return idlers, impact idlers at the loading point, training (self-aligning) idlers. Take-up: gravity or screw. Keeps belt tension. Belt cleaners (primary and secondary scrapers), skirts and seals. Pull-wire emergency stops, belt sway switches, speed sensors.

A belt moves toward the end of the idler it touches first. It steers away from the high side. Check the structure is square and level, and the belt splice is square. Check all idlers are square to the belt and turning. Start at the head end and work along the return side, then the carrying side. Move the idler end forward (in the direction of belt travel) on the side the belt runs toward. Small moves, one idler at a time. Use pulleys for tracking only as a last resort. The constant level oiler was empty. Why was it empty? It isn't on the lube route. Why isn't it on the route? The pump was installed last year and the route was never updated. Root cause: no process to add new equipment to lube routes. Fix: add an MOC/handover step that updates the PM and lube routes.
List possible causes on branches: Machine, Method, Material, Man (people), Measurement, Environment . Then test each one against the evidence. Cross out the ones the evidence disproves.

What happened (one paragraph, facts only). Impact (safety, production, cost). Timeline. Evidence (photos, measurements, data). Analysis (5 Whys, fishbone). Root causes (physical, human, latent). Actions: owner, due date, how we'll know it worked. Blame-free. People hide facts when they fear punishment. Focus on how the system let it happen.

t: Steel metallurgy for welders › Heat-affected zone (HAZ)
x: The base metal next to the weld that was heated but not melted. Its grain structure changes. Fast cooling of hardenable steel forms martensite : hard and brittle. HAZ hardness limits are often 248 HV10 for sour service (NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 at 22 HRC) and 325–350 HV for general service.

t: Steel metallurgy for welders › Hydrogen (cold) cracking
x: Needs three things together: hydrogen, a hard microstructure and stress. Appears hours (up to 48 h) after welding, in the HAZ or weld metal. Remove one factor: Low-hydrogen consumables, dry and clean joints. Preheat and interpass temperature to slow cooling and let hydrogen escape. Post-heat (hydrogen bake-out, e.g. 200–300 °C for 2 h) straight after welding on critical joints. Reduce restraint, good fit-up. Delay final NDT (often 24–48 h) on susceptible steels.

t: Steel metallurgy for welders › Hot (solidification) cracking
x: Centreline cracks during solidification. Caused by sulphur and phosphorus, deep narrow beads, high restraint. Austenitic stainless fillers contain some ferrite (FN 3–10) to resist it. Fix: bead shape width ≥ depth, fill craters, clean base metal.

t: Steel metallurgy for welders › Lamellar tearing
x: Step-like cracks in plate under T-joints loaded through thickness. Use Z-grade plate (through-thickness tested), buttering, joint design that spreads load.

t: Steel metallurgy for welders › Stainless problems
x: Sensitisation : chromium carbides form at 450–850 °C, leaving chromium-poor zones that corrode (weld decay). Use L grades (≤ 0.03% C) or stabilised (321, 347). Keep heat input and interpass low. Sigma phase : brittle phase from long time at 600–900 °C. Distortion : stainless expands 50% more than carbon steel and conducts heat poorly. Contamination : carbon steel tools and grinding discs leave iron that rusts. Use stainless-only brushes and discs.

Has prequalified WPSs that don't need testing if all the rules are followed. ISO 15614-1 (procedures) and ISO 9606-1 (welders) in Europe and many other regions. API 1104 : pipelines.

t: WPS, PQR & WPQ › What a WPS shows
x: Process(es), type (manual, semi-auto). Joint design: groove type, angle, root gap, land, backing. Base metals: P-numbers / groups, thickness range, diameter range. Filler metals: specification (SFA), classification, F-number, A-number, size. Positions and progression. Preheat min, interpass max. PWHT: temperature and time range, or none. Gas: type, flow, backing gas. Electrical: current type and polarity, amps, volts, travel speed, heat input range. Technique: stringer or weave, cleaning method, back gouging, peening.

Changing an essential variable beyond its range needs a new PQR. Changing a supplementary essential variable needs a new PQR only where toughness (impact) testing is required. Non-essential variables can change by revising the WPS. Typical essential variables (ASME IX) Process change Base metal P-number change (outside allowed groupings) Thickness outside qualified range Filler F-number or A-number change Preheat decrease more than 55 °C (100 °F) PWHT added, removed, or changed temperature range Shielding gas change (GTAW/GMAW) in some cases Heat input increase (when impact tested) — supplemen

Heat input (kJ/mm) = (Volts × Amps × 60) ÷ (Travel speed mm/min × 1000) ISO adds a thermal efficiency factor k (0.8 for SMAW/GMAW/FCAW, 0.6 for GTAW, 1.0 for SAW). Example: 24 V, 140 A, 150 mm/min = 1.34 kJ/mm (arc energy).

Make sure every welder has the right WPS at the joint and is qualified for it (process, position, thickness, diameter, F-number). Check preheat and interpass with a contact thermometer or crayons. Check consumables match the WPS and are stored properly. Keep the weld log (weld map): joint number, welder stamp, WPS, date, NDT required and result, repair number. Welders stamp or mark their ID next to each weld (low-stress stamps or paint marker, per spec).

k: preheat interpass post heat dehydrogenation pwht stress relief heating rate cooling rate soak time thermocouple induction resistance heating ceramic pads b31.3 table 331 temperature crayon tempilstik

x: Preheat slows the cooling rate, so less hard martensite forms and hydrogen can diffuse out. It also drives off moisture. Apply with gas torches (rosebud), electric resistance pads or induction coils. Heat a band at least 75 mm (3") each side of the joint, or 4× thickness (some codes), through the full thickness. Measure on the side opposite the heat source where possible, or wait 1 minute per 25 mm thickness after removing the torch (ISO 13916 rule). Use contact thermometers, thermocouples or temperature indicating crayons. A crayon rated at the temperature melts when the steel reaches it.

t: Preheat, interpass & PWHT › Typical minimum preheat (guide, always follow WPS)
x: Material Thickness Minimum preheat P1 carbon steel, C ≤ 0.30% ≤ 25 mm 10 °C (warm to dry if wet or cold) P1 carbon steel 25 mm, or high CE 80–100 °C P3 (C-½Mo) All 80 °C P4 (1¼Cr-½Mo) All 120–150 °C P5A (2¼Cr-1Mo) All 150–200 °C P5B (5Cr, 9Cr) All 200 °C+ P91 All 200–250 °C, max interpass ~300 °C P8 austenitic stainless All None (just dry). Interpass max ~150–175 °C

Minimum interpass = minimum preheat. Don't let the joint cool below it until the weld is done (or post-heated). Maximum interpass protects toughness and corrosion resistance: often 250–315 °C for carbon steel, 150–175 °C for stainless, 100–150 °C for duplex.
Right after welding, before the joint cools, raise it to around 200–300 °C and hold for 1–4 hours (by procedure). Common on thick Cr-Mo and high-restraint joints that can't go straight into PWHT.

t: Preheat, interpass & PWHT › PWHT (post weld heat treatment)
x: Heating the completed weld to below the lower critical temperature to relieve residual stresses and temper the HAZ. Material (B31.3 / ASME VIII guide) When required Temperature Hold time P1 carbon steel Nominal thickness 19 mm (3/4") (older B31.3 Table 331.1.1; newer editions differ) 595–650 °C 1 h per 25 mm, min 1 h P3 19 mm or specified UTS high 595–720 °C 1 h/25 mm, min 1 h P4 13 mm or as code 705–745 °C 1 h/25 mm, min 2 h P5A, P5B Most thicknesses 705–760 °C 1 h/25 mm, min 2 h P91 (15E) Always 730–775 °C 1 h/25 mm, min 2 h P8 stainless Normally not required – – Code tables change between e

t: Preheat, interpass & PWHT › Heating and cooling rates
x: Above 315–425 °C, control heating and cooling. A common rule: max rate (°C/h) = 220 × 25 ÷ thickness (mm), not more than 220 °C/h and not less than 55 °C/h. Below the control temperature (often 300–425 °C) cool in still air under insulation.

t: Preheat, interpass & PWHT › Thermocouples and band widths
x: Soak band: weld width plus at least 1 t (thickness) or 25 mm each side, whichever is less (B31.3 says weld plus 25 mm each side minimum; AWS D10.10 gives more detail). Heated band and insulation band wider (insulation band often soak band + 4 × √(R t)). Attach thermocouples by capacitor discharge welding. Usually at least 2 per joint (top and bottom for horizontal pipe), more for large pipe. Record the full chart: heating, soak, cooling, with time scale and thermocouple ID.

All welding, including attachments, finished. Welding after PWHT means doing it again. NDT done if required before PWHT. Support the piping: strength drops at temperature and the pipe can sag. Remove valves, instruments and soft materials from the heat zone. Open ends closed to stop chimney effect (draught cooling the inside).
Hardness test (often required: e.g. ≤ 225 HB for P4/P5, ≤ 241 HB for some Cr-Mo, ≤ 200 HB for sour carbon steel). Final NDT if specified after PWHT. Attach the chart to the weld record.

k: distortion shrinkage angular distortion bowing buckling longitudinal transverse backstep skip welding presetting strongback clamp flame straightening heat straightening
x: Weld metal shrinks as it cools. The surrounding metal resists. The result is either distortion (movement) or residual stress (locked-in). Usually both.

Transverse shrinkage : across the weld. Longitudinal shrinkage : along the weld (causes bowing on long members). Angular distortion : plates fold toward the weld side (single-sided V welds and fillets). Bowing / camber : long beams curve. Buckling : thin plates go wavy. Rotational : gap closes or opens as the weld progresses.

Don't overweld. A 6 mm fillet where 8 mm is welded puts in 78% more weld metal than needed. Use intermittent welds where allowed. Use double-sided joints (X prep) and balance welding about the neutral axis. Place welds near the neutral axis. Use fewer passes with larger beads (less angular distortion, but watch heat input limits). Use J or U preps on thick plate (less weld metal).

Presetting : set the parts slightly the opposite way so shrinkage pulls them square. Example: preset a T-joint flange 1–2° outward. Back-to-back assembly: clamp two identical parts together and weld both. Strongbacks and clamps : hold the joint. Release after cooling. Backstep welding : weld short segments in the opposite direction to the overall progression. Skip welding : weld short lengths spaced apart, then fill in. Balanced sequence : alternate sides on double-V joints. On pipe flanges, weld opposite quadrants. Peening (if allowed by the WPS): stretches the bead to counter shrinkage. Not

Mechanical : presses, jacks, clamps. Cold working may need engineering approval for pressure parts. Flame (heat) straightening : heat spots, lines or wedges (V-heats) on the long side to make it shrink. Carbon steel: keep below about 650 °C (dull red). Q T steels: lower limits, often 600 °C or less. Stainless: limited. Let it cool naturally. Water quenching only where the material allows.

t: Distortion control › Flange and pipe distortion
x: Weld-neck flanges pull out of square during welding. Check face squareness with a flange square after root and hot pass and adjust sequence. Slip-on flanges: weld the inside fillet and outside fillet alternately in quadrants. Leave spools long on one end for final fit-up (field weld with extra length).

t: Welding stainless & duplex › Keep it clean
x: Separate stainless fabrication from carbon steel. Free iron from carbon steel tools rusts on stainless. Use stainless wire brushes and dedicated grinding discs (iron-free, labelled for stainless). No carbon steel slings or chains; use nylon or protect with plastic. Clean with acetone or chloride-free solvent. No marker pens with chlorides or sulphur. Store on wooden or plastic racks, not steel.

No preheat. Max interpass about 150–175 °C. Low heat input: stringer beads, fast travel. Back purge the root (argon) for GTAW roots, or use flux-cored backing products. Use L-grade fillers for corrosion resistance. Expect distortion: tack closer, clamp, balance sequence.

t: Welding stainless & duplex › Duplex (2205) and super duplex (2507)
x: Target ferrite 30–65% (ferrite scope test on weld and HAZ). Heat input usually 0.5–2.5 kJ/mm for 2205 (0.2–1.5 for 2507). Too low: too much ferrite. Too high: intermetallic phases. Interpass max typically 150 °C (2205) and 100 °C (2507). Use over-alloyed filler (2209, 2594) for the right phase balance. Purge with argon or argon + 2% nitrogen; O₂ 50 ppm typical. Corrosion test (ASTM G48) and impact tests often on the PQR.
Preheat 200–300 °C. PWHT required (often 650–760 °C). Or use austenitic filler (309) for repairs where PWHT isn't possible (with engineering approval).

t: Welding stainless & duplex › After welding: pickling and passivation
x: Remove heat tint with pickling paste (nitric/hydrofluoric acid) or electrochemical cleaning. Mechanical brushing alone leaves a weak layer. Passivate (nitric or citric acid) to rebuild the protective chromium oxide layer. Rinse with low-chloride water. Neutralise and dispose of acid waste correctly. Pickling acids are very hazardous: full PPE (face shield, acid gloves, apron), with calcium gluconate gel available for HF exposure.

t: Cr-Mo, P91 & dissimilar welds › Chrome-moly steels (P11, P22, P5)
x: Used in high temperature steam, hydrogen and refinery heater service. Prone to hydrogen cracking: low-hydrogen consumables, controlled preheat, interpass, post-heat and PWHT. Match filler chemistry to the base metal. PWHT is almost always required. Hardness checks after. Material verification (PMI with XRF) on every component: a carbon steel elbow in a P22 line fails quickly.

t: Cr-Mo, P91 & dissimilar welds › P91 / Grade 91 (9Cr-1Mo-V)
x: Creep strength enhanced ferritic steel. Excellent strength at 550–620 °C, but unforgiving. Preheat 200–250 °C. Maintain throughout. Interpass max typically 300–350 °C. After welding, cool to below about 100 °C (to complete martensite transformation) unless the procedure says hold, but not to ambient before PWHT if hydrogen risk. Follow the specific procedure. PWHT 730–775 °C promptly. Wrong PWHT (too high or too low) ruins creep strength. Hardness after PWHT typically 190–250 HB (spec dependent). Too soft is as bad as too hard. Ni + Mn in filler limited (e.g. ≤ 1.0–1.2%) to keep the transforma

t: Cr-Mo, P91 & dissimilar welds › Dissimilar metal welds (DMW)
x: Carbon steel to stainless : 309L filler for low temperature service. Carbon migrates at high temperature, so above about 315–425 °C use nickel filler (ERNiCr-3). Buttering : lay a layer of the right filler on one side (often the ferritic side), PWHT if needed, then make the closing weld without PWHT. Dilution: the first pass mixes base and filler. Check the Schaeffler or WRC-1992 diagram for the resulting structure (aim for some ferrite in austenitic deposits, avoid martensite). Thermal expansion mismatch causes fatigue at high temperature cycles. Place DMWs in low-stress locations.
Positive material identification by XRF or OES confirms alloy content of pipe, fittings, bolts and weld metal. Mandatory on alloy systems on most refinery projects (API RP 578).

k: aluminium aluminum welding oxide ac tig balance pulse mig push pull spool gun 4043 5356 6061 hot cracking porosity hydrogen
x: Melts at about 660 °C, but its oxide melts at about 2,050 °C. The oxide must be removed: stainless brush (aluminium only) and solvent just before welding. Conducts heat about 4–5× faster than steel: needs more current, and the weld can suddenly sink through. No colour change before melting. Porosity comes from hydrogen: moisture, oil, damp filler. Keep rods sealed and clean.

AC with balance control: more electrode-positive time for cleaning, more negative for penetration (typical 65–75% EN). Pure, zirconiated or lanthanated tungsten. Argon, or argon/helium for thicker sections.
Spray or pulsed spray, 100% argon (Ar/He for thick). Soft wire: use push-pull or spool gun, U-groove rolls, PTFE liner, contact tip oversize. Push technique (forehand) 10–15°.
Heat-treatable alloys (6061-T6) lose up to 30–40% strength in the HAZ. Design must allow for it. Keep preheat and interpass low (often ≤ 120 °C, max 150 °C). Don't hold at temperature.
6xxx alloys are crack sensitive without filler. Always add filler (4043 or 5356) to change the chemistry. Fill craters at the end of each weld; use crater fill function.

x: Preheat flame heats steel to ignition (about 870 °C, bright red). A jet of pure oxygen burns the iron. Works only on carbon and low alloy steel (not stainless, aluminium, cast iron). Plate thickness Nozzle (typical) Oxygen (bar) Speed (mm/min) 6 mm 1/32" (0.8 mm) 2.0 500–650 12 mm 3/64" (1.2 mm) 2.5 400–550 25 mm 1/16" (1.6 mm) 3.0 300–400 50 mm 5/64" (2.0 mm) 3.5 200–300 100 mm 3/32" (2.4 mm) 4.0–5.0 130–180 Figures vary a lot by nozzle maker and fuel. Use the nozzle chart. Acetylene: hottest flame, fastest preheat. Max working pressure 1 bar (15 psi). Propane: cheaper, slower preheat, more o

Cuts any electrically conductive metal: carbon steel, stainless, aluminium, copper. Air plasma common for up to about 25–40 mm (hand-held). Mechanised with O₂ or N₂/H₂ mixes for quality cuts. Narrow kerf, small HAZ, fast on thin and medium plate. Consumables: electrode and nozzle wear. Replace both together when the cut quality drops. Dry, clean air supply essential. Eye protection: shade 8–11 depending on current.

t: Cutting & gouging › Air carbon arc gouging (arc-air)
x: A copper-coated carbon electrode makes an arc; compressed air (5.5–7 bar) blows the molten metal away. Used for back gouging, removing defects, removing welds. DCEP, high current (e.g. 9.5 mm rod at 350–450 A). Electrode angle about 35–45°, air jet behind the arc on the cutting side. Grind 1–2 mm after gouging carbon steel to remove the carbon-enriched layer before rewelding. On stainless, avoid or grind more. Very loud (over 100 dB) and lots of molten spray: hearing and fire protection, clear the area.

t: Cutting & gouging › Mechanical cutting and bevelling
x: Pipe bevelling machines (clamshell / split frame, ID-mounted): best bevel quality for alloy and stainless. Band saws : square cuts, all materials. Abrasive cut-off discs : quick, watch disc rating and guard. Wheel pipe cutters : small bore, leave a burr inside to remove. Thermal cutting of alloy steels (Cr-Mo, P91) usually needs preheat and removal of 1.5–3 mm of the HAZ by grinding or machining afterwards.

k: plate rolling bending press brake roll bending three roll four roll pre bending springback minimum bend radius cold forming hot forming flat pattern

x: Three-roll pyramid : leaves flat ends that must be pre-bent (press or rolls) or cut off. Four-roll and double-pinch three-roll : pre-bend the ends in the machine. Roll in several passes, checking with a template (sweep board) cut to the inside radius. Template length at least 1/6 of the circumference or 600 mm. Clean rolls and plate: scale and weld spatter mark the plate. Roll with the plate rolling direction (grain) parallel to the roll axis where possible.

t: Rolling, bending & forming › Cold forming limits
x: For pressure parts (ASME VIII UCS-79), cold forming that strains carbon steel more than 5% may need heat treatment (with conditions). Fibre strain for a cylinder rolled from flat plate: Strain % = 50 × t ÷ Rf t = thickness, Rf = final centreline radius. Example: 25 mm plate rolled to 500 mm radius: 50 × 25 ÷ 500 = 2.5%.

t: Rolling, bending & forming › Press brake bending
x: Die opening (V) typically 6–8× thickness for mild steel up to ~10 mm; 10–12× for thicker. Inside bend radius about V/6 to V/8 in air bending. Springback: mild steel 1–2°, stainless 2–4°, high strength more. Over-bend to compensate. Minimum inside radius: about 1× thickness for mild steel, 1.5–2× for higher strength or bending across the grain of some plate. Bend with the bend line across the rolling direction (perpendicular to the grain) to reduce cracking.

t: Rolling, bending & forming › Flat pattern (bend allowance)
x: Bend allowance = θ (rad) × (R + K × t) K-factor about 0.33 for tight bends, 0.5 for large radii (mild steel ~0.4 in air bending). Flat length = sum of straight legs (to the bend tangent lines) + bend allowances.

Carbon steel: 900–1,050 °C, work above about 750 °C. Don't work in the blue brittle range (200–400 °C). Heads and fittings formed hot are then normalised. Q T steels and stainless have special limits.

k: layout marking out pattern development cone layout eccentric reducer lobster back mitre bend segmented elbow branch template saddle cutting geometry circumference chord

x: Circumference = π × D Chord = 2 × R × sin(θ/2) Arc = R × θ (rad) Divide a circle into 12 or 16 equal parts for pattern work. Chord for 12 divisions = R (radius stepped around). 3-4-5 triangle for squaring: 3 m, 4 m, 5 m (or multiples). Check rectangles by diagonals: equal diagonals = square corners.

t: Layout & pattern development › Cut length of pipe for wraparounds
x: Wraparound (template) length = π × OD. Divide into ordinates (e.g. 16 equal strips) for marking profiles.

t: Layout & pattern development › Concentric cone (reducer) layout
x: Large diameter D, small diameter d, height H (use mean diameters for thick plate). Full cone height (to the apex): H' = H × D ÷ (D − d). Slant height of the full cone: L = √(H'² + (D/2)²). Inner arc radius: l = L × d ÷ D. Developed angle: θ = 360° × (D/2) ÷ L. Draw two arcs of radius L and l from the same centre, mark angle θ. That's the flat pattern. Example: D = 1000, d = 500, H = 400. H' = 400 × 1000 ÷ 500 = 800. L = √(800² + 500²) = 943. l = 471.5. θ = 360 × 500 ÷ 943 = 190.9°.

t: Layout & pattern development › Segmented (lobster-back / mitre) bends
x: A 90° bend in n segments has 2 end half-segments and (n − 2) full segments, with (n − 1) welds. Cut angle on each segment end = bend angle ÷ (2 × number of welds). For 90° with 3 welds (4 pieces): 90 ÷ 6 = 15° per cut face, each full segment 30° total. Segment back length (outside) = (R + OD/2) × 2 × tan(cut angle); throat (inside) = (R − OD/2) × 2 × tan(cut angle). B31.3 limits mitre bends: angle change per weld over 22.5° is limited to low-pressure service.

t: Layout & pattern development › Pipe branch (saddle) template
x: For a branch of radius r on a header of radius R at 90°: Ordinate height h(θ) = R − √(R² − (r × sin θ)²) Divide the branch circumference into 16 equal parts (θ = 0°, 22.5°, 45° … 360°). Calculate h for each θ. The cut line on the branch is h below a straight reference line. Plot on a paper wrap of length π × OD (branch), join the points smoothly, wrap and mark. The hole in the header: width = 2r along the header axis, and use the same method on the header. Example: 4" branch (r = 57.15) on 8" header (R = 109.55): at θ = 90°, h = 109.55 − √(109.55² − 57.15²) = 16.1 mm. At 0° and 180°, h = 0.

Soapstone or silver pencil for hot or rough work; scriber and centre punch for accurate lines. Paint markers (low chloride for stainless). Wrap-arounds (flexible steel or fibreglass bands) for square cuts on pipe. Centre head and pipe centring tools for marking branch centres. Laser levels and plumb lines for site layout.

k: welding safety fume extraction hexavalent chromium manganese uv flash arc eye shade number electric shock fire watch hot work gas cylinder flashback arrestor ppe

x: All welding fume is a carcinogen (IARC Group 1). Use local exhaust ventilation (LEV) at the arc, or fume extraction guns. Stainless welding fume contains hexavalent chromium and nickel. Use LEV and respiratory protection (powered air respirator). Galvanised steel: zinc fume causes metal fume fever. Remove the coating or extract and protect. Manganese from many electrodes: neurological damage over long exposure. Degreaser vapour (chlorinated solvents) near the arc can form phosgene. Keep apart.

Process / current Lens shade (EN 169 / ANSI Z49.1 guide) SMAW 60 A 7–9 SMAW 60–160 A 10 SMAW 160–250 A 11–12 SMAW 250 A 12–14 GTAW 50 A 8–10 GTAW 50–150 A 10–12 GTAW 150 A 12–14 GMAW / FCAW 60–160 A 10–11 GMAW / FCAW 160–250 A 12 Plasma cutting 300 A 8–9 Oxy-fuel cutting 3–6 (goggles) Air carbon arc gouging 12–14 Welding screens to protect others from flash. Cover skin: UV burns like sunburn in minutes. Arc eye: gritty, painful eyes hours after exposure. Get first aid.

Inspect leads and holders daily. Replace damaged insulation. Dry gloves. Don't stand in water. Use insulated mats in wet locations. Use voltage reduction devices (VRD) in confined or wet spaces. Earth (return) clamp close to the weld, on clean metal. Never earth through bearings, chains or pipe racks carrying others' work. Switch off and remove rods when leaving the station.

Hot work permit and gas test. Clear combustibles within 11 m (35 ft) or cover with fire blankets. Fire watch during work and at least 30 minutes after (often 60 min on some sites). Cover drains, openings and gratings where sparks can fall. Extinguisher at hand.

Store upright, chained, valve caps on, in ventilated areas. Separate oxygen from fuel gases by 6 m or a 1.5 m high fire wall (30 min rated). Flashback arrestors at the regulator outlets on both oxygen and fuel. Check valves at the torch. Leak test with leak detection fluid, never a flame. Open cylinder valves slowly, stand to the side of the regulator. Acetylene cylinder valves open max 1½ turns, keep the key on the valve. Never use oxygen to blow dust off or to ventilate. Oxygen-enriched clothing burns violently. Close cylinders and bleed hoses at the end of the shift.

Helmet with correct shade (auto-darkening checked), safety glasses under it. Flame-resistant clothing, leather jacket or sleeves for overhead. Leather welding gloves (TIG gloves thinner). Safety boots with no exposed laces; spats for heavy spatter. Hearing protection for gouging and grinding. Respiratory protection as the fume assessment requires.

t: Pipe sizes & schedules › NPS and DN
x: NPS (nominal pipe size, inches) and DN (metric nominal) are names, not measurements. DN 100 = NPS 4. For NPS ⅛ to 12, OD is bigger than the NPS number. From NPS 14 up, OD (in inches) = NPS. All pipe of one NPS has the same OD. The schedule changes the wall and therefore the ID. Carbon steel: ASME B36.10M. Stainless: ASME B36.19M (schedules with "S": 5S, 10S, 40S, 80S).
Weight (kg/m) = 0.02466 × t × (OD − t) (mm, carbon steel) Example: 6" Sch 40: 0.02466 × 7.11 × (168.3 − 7.11) = 28.26 kg/m. Stainless is about 1–2% heavier.
Seamless pipe wall can be up to 12.5% under nominal (ASTM A106/A53). Design calculations deduct it. Measure actual wall with UT where it matters.

Stencil along the pipe shows: maker, specification and grade (A106 Gr B), size and schedule, heat number, test pressure (or NH = non-hydrotested), seamless (SMLS) or welded (ERW, SAW), and dual certification if any (A106 B / A53 B / API 5L B). Keep the heat number on every cut piece (transfer it before cutting).

t: Fittings & take-outs › Elbows at other angles
x: Take-out = R × tan(θ / 2) R = 1.5 × NPS × 25.4 for LR 6" LR elbow cut to 60°: 228.6 × tan 30° = 132 mm.

Concentric : centrelines match. Vertical lines and general use. Eccentric : one side flat. Pump suctions (flat side on top to avoid air pockets), pipe racks (flat on bottom to keep bottom of pipe level).

t: Fittings & take-outs › Socket weld and threaded (ASME B16.11)
x: Classes 3000, 6000, 9000 (socket weld) and 2000, 3000, 6000 (threaded). Usually NPS 2 and smaller. Socket weld gap : pull the pipe back about 1.6 mm (1/16") from the socket bottom before welding to allow for shrinkage. Use a gap ring or mark the pipe. Fillet weld size: B31.3 asks for a minimum leg of 1.25 × nominal pipe wall, or the socket wall thickness if that is smaller. Not for severe cyclic service or where crevice corrosion matters.

Tees (equal and reducing): best for strength. Weldolet (butt weld), sockolet (socket), threadolet (threaded), elbolet (on elbows), latrolet (45°), nipolet . Stub-in (set-on or set-in branch) with or without reinforcing pad, per code calculation. Branch hole: cut and bevel to give full penetration access. Remove the coupon.

Cheap, easy to align. t: Gaskets › Ring joint gaskets (API 6A / ASME B16.20)
x: R : oval or octagonal. Octagonal seals better and is common. Oval fits old round-bottom grooves too. RX : pressure-energised, for API 6A flanges. BX : pressure-energised for 10,000 psi+ API 6BX flanges, face-to-face contact. Ring must be softer than the groove (soft iron, low carbon steel, 4–6% Cr, 304, 316). Hardness stamped on the ring. Never reuse ring joints.

Kammprofile (camprofile) : serrated metal core with graphite or PTFE facing. Excellent for heat exchangers and high-cycle services. Compressed non-asbestos fibre (CNAF) : water, low pressure steam, utilities. Class 150 to 300 low temperature. Flexible graphite sheet (with metal insert): high temperature, good chemical resistance, not for strong oxidisers. PTFE (filled or expanded): chemicals. Cold-flows, needs good bolting. New gasket every time. Check the size, class and material stamping against the line class or spec. Store flat, in the original packaging. Don't hang spiral wound gaskets on nails. No grease or compound on spiral wound or graphite gaskets unless the maker says so. Gasket must be centred: the outer ring touches the bolts.

x: Most flange leaks are caused by uneven or insufficient bolt load, damaged faces, wrong gaskets or misaligned flanges. A controlled bolt-up fixes most of them.

Check flange faces for damage. Clean with a non-metallic brush. Check flange alignment (PCC-1 guide): centreline offset ≤ 1.5 mm, gap parallelism ≤ 0.8 mm difference, rotational alignment within 3 mm at bolt holes, gap no more than twice the gasket thickness. Don't force flanges together with bolts. Check gasket type, size, rating. Check stud and nut grade and length (one to three threads through the nut). Clean and lubricate threads and the nut bearing face with the specified lubricant. Note its nut factor K. Number the bolts clockwise (1, 2, 3 …).

t: Flange bolting (ASME PCC-1) › Legacy cross-pattern sequence (PCC-1)
x: Install : hand tighten, then snug to 20–30 N·m (not more than 20% of target). Check the gap is even. Round 1 : 20–30% of target torque, cross pattern. Round 2 : 50–70% of target, cross pattern. Round 3 : 100% of target, cross pattern. Round 4 : 100% in a circular (rotational) pattern, clockwise, until nuts no longer turn. Round 5 (optional): 100% circular after at least 4 hours (relaxation check). Measure gaps at 4 or 8 places between rounds. Correct uneven gaps in the next round. PCC-1 also gives faster alternative patterns (e.g. quadrant patterns) that work well on large flanges with many bo

x: Stretches the stud directly with a hydraulic tool. Load is not affected by friction. Needs longer studs (one extra diameter of thread above the nut). Tension 50% or 100% of the bolts at once. With 50% coverage, do two passes plus a check pass. Account for load loss when the tool is released (load transfer factor), per the calculation.

t: Flange bolting (ASME PCC-1) › Joint integrity records
x: Tag each joint after make-up: joint ID, gasket, bolt material, torque/tension value, tool serial, date, technician, verifier. Critical joints (high pressure, toxic, hot): independent verification and sign-off before leak test. Bolting technicians trained and qualified (PCC-1 Appendix A). Never tighten or loosen flange bolts on a pressurised joint (hot bolting only under a specific, approved procedure with half the bolts at a time).

x: Latest revision? Check the revision cloud and title block. Line class and BOM match the spec. Dimensions add up: sum of segments = overall dimension between coordinates. Valve orientation (stem, flow direction) and handwheel access. Branch and instrument connection sizes and ratings. Weld numbering, NDT requirements and PWHT notes. Field weld locations sensible for transport and fit-up.

x: Iso received, checked, material issued with heat numbers. Cut list: pipe lengths, fitting take-outs, bevels. Cut and bevel. Transfer heat numbers to every cut piece. Fit-up: check gap, hi-lo, alignment, orientation. QC hold point on critical lines. Welding per WPS. Weld log updated. Dimensional check against iso. NDT per percentage required. PWHT if required. Internal cleaning, blowout, end caps. Painting or coating (except weld areas for field test if required). Spool tagged (spool number, line number, iso) and dispatched.

t: Spool fabrication & erection › Fabrication tolerances (typical, e.g. PFI ES-3)
x: Linear dimensions (face to face, centre to face): ±3 mm (±1/8"). Flange face tilt: 0.15 mm per 25 mm of flange OD (max 0.4° approx), or 1/16" across face per site spec. Flange bolt hole rotation: ±1.5 mm (1/16"). Branch location: ±1.5 mm. Out of plane / overall: ±3–5 mm depending on spool size.

Erect from fixed points (equipment nozzles) toward the free end. Anchor points first. Set spools on temporary supports. Don't hang spools off equipment nozzles. Use field welds with extra length to cut to fit. Connecting to rotating equipment : make the final flange connection last. Flanges must line up without force (pipe strain check with dial indicators on the coupling). Typical alignment: parallel within 0.25 mm across the face, offset ≤ 0.5 mm, bolts drop in freely. Cold spring only if the design specifies it, with exact gap measured and recorded. Install permanent supports and spring han

Variable spring: load changes with movement. Cold and hot load marked on the nameplate. Constant spring: same load over full travel. Set to the cold position, remove travel stops after hydrotest and before start-up. Check hot position after start-up and record.

Fill from the low point with clean water (for stainless: chlorides 50 ppm, often 2

t: Pressure testing › Pneumatic test extra rules
x: Needs owner approval and a safety assessment of stored energy and exclusion distance. Leak check welds by soap solution or by sensitive method before raising pressure. Raise to 25% (or 1.7 bar) first for a preliminary check, then in steps of 10% of test pressure. Nobody inside the exclusion zone during pressurising and hold. Stored energy in gas is enormous. A pneumatic test failure can throw fragments hundreds of metres. Even on hydrotests, trapped air pockets store energy. Vent thoroughly.

t: Flushing, blowing & cleaning › Lube oil flushing
x: Bypass bearings and seals: install jumpers so flush oil doesn't pass through machine internals. Use flushing oil (or the service oil) heated to 60–70 °C to lower viscosity. Aim for turbulent flow: Reynolds number 4,000 (often flow 2–3× normal using a flushing rig). Cycle temperature hot/cold, and hammer or vibrate the pipes at welds and bends to loosen debris. Fit fine filters (5–10 µm) and temporary screens (100 mesh) at bearing inlets. Sample at set intervals. Continue until particle count reaches the target for the specified time (e.g. 3 consecutive samples at 12 h interval). Drain flushing

Use temporary piping and a silencer at the outlet, in a fenced exclusion zone. Cycle: heat the line, blow at a disturbance factor (ratio of blow momentum to normal) ≥ 1.2–1.4, then cool. The cooling cycles loosen scale. Install target plates near the end after several blows to check. Noise over 130 dB: notify neighbours, hearing protection.

t: Small bore, threaded & tubing › Threaded pipe
x: NPT (ASME B1.20.1): 60° taper threads, 1:16 taper. Seal is in the threads, needs sealant. BSPT (ISO 7/EN 10226): 55° taper. Not interchangeable with NPT. BSPP (ISO 228): parallel, seals on a bonded washer or O-ring, not on the thread. Hand-tight engagement plus 2–3 turns by wrench for NPT (small sizes). Don't over-tighten (cracks fittings). PTFE tape: 2–3 wraps clockwise looking at the thread end, start 1 thread back. Not on the first thread, so tape doesn't get into the system. Or use anaerobic or PTFE paste sealant. Seal welding of threaded joints: remove all sealant first and use a qualifie

t: Small bore, threaded & tubing › Small bore connections (SBC)
x: Vents, drains, instrument tappings and sample points cause many plant leaks from vibration fatigue. Keep the overhung mass short: valve close to the parent pipe. Brace SBCs on vibrating lines (pumps, compressors) back to the parent pipe, not to independent steel. Use full-penetration weldolets or sockolets rated for the service, and 2:1 fillet profile on socket welds in vibrating service. Close and plug (or cap) all vent and drain valves with a plug of the right rating. Survey with the Energy Institute SBC guidelines.

t: Small bore, threaded & tubing › Instrument tubing
x: Common: 316 SS seamless, annealed, ASTM A269. Sizes 1/4", 3/8", 1/2" OD (or 6, 10, 12 mm). Wall thickness by pressure: 1/2" × 0.049" is common for impulse lines up to about 3,000+ psi; check maker's tables. Don't mix inch and metric fittings and tube. Metric fittings often have a step marking on the nut. Cut square with a tube cutter, deburr inside and out.

t: Small bore, threaded & tubing › Two-ferrule compression fittings (Swagelok, Parker A-Lok type)
x: Insert the tube fully until it bottoms in the fitting body. Nut finger tight. Mark the nut at the 6 o'clock position. Hold the body with a wrench. Tighten the nut 1¼ turns for 1/4" and larger (¾ turn for 1/16"–3/16" sizes). Check with a gap inspection gauge: the gauge must not enter the gap between nut and body (on brands that use gauges). Re-make: tighten to the original position, then about 1/4 turn more. Never mix components from different makers. Each design is matched.

t: Small bore, threaded & tubing › Tube bending and support
x: Use a proper bender. Minimum bend radius from the bender (often 3× OD). Leave a straight length at the fitting (at least the fitting depth plus a margin) so the tube enters straight. Support tubing at intervals: 1/4" every 0.9 m, 1/2" every 1.5 m (typical). Slope impulse lines per hook-up drawing (liquid lines down to the transmitter, gas lines up).

x: Sizes by OD and SDR (standard dimension ratio = OD ÷ wall). SDR 11 is common for pressure water (PN16 for PE100). Butt fusion : face both ends with the facer, check alignment, heat with the plate (≈ 210–230 °C), remove plate quickly, join at the specified fusion pressure, hold for the cooling time. Follow ISO 21307 or the maker's table. Log every weld (data logger). Electrofusion : couplers with built-in heating wire. Scrape the pipe surface (remove 0.2–0.3 mm oxidised layer), clean, mark insertion depth, clamp, run the cycle. Don't touch the scraped area. Expansion is about 10× steel. Allow f

Solvent cement: cut square, deburr and chamfer, clean with primer, apply cement to both, push in with a quarter turn, hold 30 s. Cure time before pressure depends on size and temperature (hours to a day). Never air test PVC: it shatters. UV degrades PVC: paint or protect outdoors.

Joints: adhesive bonded (taper/taper or spigot/socket), laminated (butt and wrap), or flanged. Only trained and certified bonders/laminators (e.g. ISO 14692 or maker certification). Control temperature and humidity during curing; use heating blankets in cold conditions. Flanges: use full-face gaskets, flat washers, and the maker's low torque values. Over-torquing cracks the flange. Protect from impact: one hammer blow can crack the liner without visible damage.

t: Non-metallic piping › Lined pipe (PTFE, PFA, PP, rubber)
x: Don't weld or flame-cut lined spools. Order to length or use spacers. Flare faces of the lining are the gasket. Protect them with covers until installation. Torque bolts to the maker's value, then re-torque after 24 h (PTFE cold flow) and after the first heat cycle. Vent holes in the steel housing let permeated gas escape. Don't paint over them. Spark test (holiday test) linings before installation if required.

x: Untied single bellows : axial movement. Needs main anchors to resist pressure thrust. Tied / universal : lateral movement, tie rods carry pressure thrust. Hinged and gimbal : angular movement in one or all planes. Pressure balanced : absorbs axial movement without thrust on anchors. Rubber (elastomer) expansion joints : water and slurry lines, pump connections. Absorb vibration and some misalignment. Need control rods where piping isn't anchored.

Install exactly at the installed (cold) length on the drawing. Never use bellows to take up misalignment or wrong pipe length. Leave the yellow shipping bars in place until the joint is installed and all supports and anchors are complete. Remove before hydrotest or start-up (as instructed by the procedure; for some tests they stay on). Flow direction arrow (for internal sleeves) must point with the flow. Protect the bellows from weld spatter, arc strikes and grinding dust. A single arc strike can cause failure. Pipe guides near the joint (first guide within 4 pipe diameters, second within 14 d

Bellows squirm (buckling sideways) means too much pressure or poor guiding. Cracks, corrosion (chlorides on stainless bellows), dents. Rubber joints: cracks, blisters, bulging. Replace typically every 5–10 years. Tie rods and limit rods nuts set as drawing.

t: Measuring tools › Reading a metric vernier (0.02 mm)
x: Read the main scale mm to the left of the vernier zero, e.g. 23 mm. Find the vernier line that lines up exactly with a main scale line, e.g. line 17. Multiply by 0.02: 17 × 0.02 = 0.34. Reading = 23.34 mm.

t: Measuring tools › Reading a metric micrometer (0.01 mm)
x: Read the sleeve: whole mm on the upper line, plus 0.5 mm if a lower half-line is visible past the last mm mark. E.g. 12.5. Read the thimble line on the sleeve centre line, e.g. 28 → 0.28. Total = 12.5 + 0.28 = 12.78 mm. Use the ratchet for consistent force. Check zero with the standard before use.

t: Measuring tools › Measuring a shaft or bore properly
x: Measure at two positions along the length and at two angles 90° apart (four readings). That shows taper and ovality. Let parts reach room temperature. Steel grows 0.0117 mm per metre per °C: a 100 mm shaft at 30 °C above ambient reads 0.035 mm big. Rock a bore gauge to find the minimum reading (true diameter), and the inside mic to find the maximum across a bore.

Set the plunger at right angles to the surface. Preload a quarter to half a turn. Use a rigid magnetic base and short arms. Lever-type (test) indicators read accurately only when the stylus is nearly parallel to the surface; angle errors are large otherwise (cosine error).
A light drag means the right size. Don't force. Stack no more than 3 leaves. Clean them; oily leaves read thicker.

Keep in cases, clean and lightly oiled. Never drop. Calibrate on a schedule (often 6–12 months) with a sticker showing due date. Don't use out-of-date tools on QC-recorded measurements. Check micrometers against standards and dial indicators against a calibrator.

t: Lathe work › Cutting speed and rpm
x: rpm = (Cutting speed m/min × 1000) ÷ (π × Diameter mm) Material HSS (m/min) Carbide (m/min) Mild steel 25–35 120–250 Medium carbon / alloy steel 15–25 90–180 Stainless (austenitic) 10–20 80–150 Cast iron 15–25 80–150 Brass / bronze 40–90 150–300 Aluminium 60–150 200–600 Example: 80 mm mild steel bar, carbide at 150 m/min: rpm = 150,000 ÷ (3.14 × 80) ≈ 600 rpm.

Three-jaw chuck: quick, self-centring, ±0.05 mm typical runout. Four-jaw independent: clock true to 0.01 mm. Best for repair work on shafts. Between centres: for long shafts. Use a steady rest for long thin work. Tool height on centre exactly. Below centre rubs, above centre digs. Keep tool overhang short.

Extend bay by bay off the stable structure. Final plumb and level, then final bolt tightening. Grout base plates (non-shrink grout, poured from one side to drive out air).

Slip-critical : pretensioned, faying surfaces prepared (clean mill scale or a Class A/B coating) so friction carries the load. No paint on faying surfaces unless qualified.

Direct tension indicators (DTI washers) : protrusions flatten at the right tension; check gaps with a feeler. Calibrated wrench : wrench set daily on a Skidmore-Wilhelm tension calibrator with sample bolts.

Don't reuse A490 or galvanised A325 bolts after pretensioning. Store bolts dry and lubricated as delivered. Rusty bolts must be cleaned and relubricated. Pre-use check by the rigger every time. Thorough examination by a competent person (often 6 months for lifting accessories). Never interpolate up. Use the next longer radius and longer boom. Total load = Load + Rigging + Hook block + (Jib/stowed items as per chart notes) Percentage of chart: total load ÷ chart capacity at the max radius × 100. Above 75–85%

Outrigger pressure = Max outrigger load ÷ Mat area Max outrigger load from the crane maker's app or a rule of thumb (up to about 75% of crane + load on one outrigger during a lift over the corner). Compare with allowable ground bearing capacity (from the civil engineer). Typical: soft clay 50–75 kPa, compact gravel 200–300 kPa, good concrete slab more (check). Use timber or composite mats sized to bring pressure below the limit. Watch for underground services, trenches, voids and edges of excavations (keep back at least the depth of the excavation).
Typical maximum for lifts 9.8 m/s (35 km/h, ~ 20 knots) at boom tip, less for large surface area loads (panels, vessels). Check the crane manual. Measure at height with the crane anemometer.

Level (within 1% or the maker's limit), outriggers fully extended as per chart, pins in. Rated capacity indicator (RCI/LMI) set for the configuration and tested. Clear swing radius, barricade. Power lines: minimum clearance by voltage (e.g. 3 m for up to 50 kV under OSHA, more in many regions; 6 m common rule). Daily inspection and log signed by the operator.

Complex / critical : over 75–85% of capacity, tandem (two cranes), over live plant or occupied areas, man-riding, near power lines, blind lifts, loads of unknown weight, lifts with special rigging, very valuable loads. Written lift plan approved by an engineer.

Load: description, weight (and source), CoG, dimensions, lifting points. Crane: type, configuration, counterweight, boom length, radius at pick and set, chart capacity, % of chart. Rigging: each item with WLL, calculated loads, sling angles. Ground: bearing capacity, mats, outrigger loads. Site plan: crane position, swing path, obstructions, exclusion zone. Weather limits. Communication: signals, radios, channel. Roles and names. Sequence step by step, including trial lift. Emergency plan.

Appointed person / lift planner : plans and approves. Lift supervisor : in charge on site. Crane operator : final say if they think the lift is unsafe. Rigger / slinger : selects and attaches rigging. Signaller / banksman : one person gives signals. Anyone can give STOP. Tagline handlers.

Go through the plan with everyone involved. Confirm weight, rigging and radius. Confirm the signaller and the signals. Check weather and wind. Walk the path and check the set-down area is ready (dunnage, bolts, people). Exclusion zone set and guarded. Trial lift: raise 100–300 mm, hold, check brakes, rigging, balance, then proceed. Stop the lift if anything changes : wind rises, load weight is different from expected, a person enters the zone, or communication fails.

Don't extend the lever. Keep the chain straight, no twists. Don't wrap the load chain around the load. Don't side load.
