x: A permit to work (PTW) is a written system that controls hazardous work. It makes sure the hazards are known, the plant is safe, the controls are in place, and everyone involved knows what is happening.

t: Permit to work › Common permit types
x: Cold work : general maintenance with no ignition sources. Hot work : welding, cutting, grinding, open flames, non-intrinsically-safe tools in hazardous areas. Confined space entry . Electrical / isolation certificate . Excavation , working at height , radiography , lifting (on some sites). Supporting certificates: isolation certificate, gas test certificate, LOTO register.

Issuing authority (IA) : usually operations. Prepares the plant, specifies controls, issues the permit. Performing authority (PA) / permit receiver : usually the supervisor. Accepts the permit, briefs the crew, makes sure conditions are followed. Area authority : owns the area, approves. Gas tester : authorised and trained.

Read the permit and all attached certificates (isolation, gas test, JSA). Walk the job with the issuer. Check isolations with your own eyes, apply your lock. Brief every crew member. Each one signs on. Display the permit at the worksite (or as site rules say). Make sure the work stays within the permit scope. New work = new permit or amendment. Stop work if conditions change (alarm, gas, weather, scope). At shift end: suspend or hand back. Leave the site safe and tidy. At job end: sign off, remove locks, return permit, confirm equipment is ready to return to service.
Face-to-face handover at the worksite where possible. Explain status: what's isolated, what's open, what's left. Incoming supervisor re-signs and re-briefs the new crew.

Simultaneous operations: when two permits or activities could affect each other (hot work near a line break, crane lift over a work area), the permits are cross-referenced and the issuer coordinates. Ask what else is happening nearby.

Operations locks all isolation points with the group locks. Keys go into a lock box. The lock box is locked by every worker with their personal lock. Nobody can remove the isolations until every worker removes their lock.

One person, one lock, one key. Never lend your key. Never remove someone else's lock. Lost key or absent worker: follow the site's lock removal procedure (manager approval, search for the person). t: Confined space entry › What is a confined space

Ventilate with air movers. Never use oxygen to ventilate. Gas test from outside at several levels (top, middle, bottom). Gases separate by density. Gas Acceptable for entry Oxygen 19.5–23.5% (some sites 20–21%) Flammable (LEL) 10% LEL (often 0% for entry; 10% for hot work outside) H₂S 1 ppm (TLV-TWA 1 ppm, STEL 5 ppm) CO 25 ppm (TLV) / 35 ppm (OSHA ceiling varies) Benzene and other toxics Below their exposure limits, specific tubes or PIDs

Manage hot work, coating and cleaning chemicals that change the atmosphere. Most confined space deaths are would-be rescuers. Never go in after a collapsed person without breathing apparatus and the rescue team.

t: Chemicals & SDS › Safety data sheet (SDS) — 16 sections
x: Most useful for the crew: Section 2 (hazards), 4 (first aid), 5 (fire), 6 (spills), 7 (handling and storage), 8 (exposure limits and PPE), 10 (stability, incompatibles).

Flame: flammable. Flame over circle: oxidiser. Exploding bomb: explosive. Corrosion: burns skin and eyes, corrodes metal. Skull and crossbones: acute toxicity. Health hazard (person with star): cancer, organ damage, sensitiser. Exclamation mark: irritant, harmful. Gas cylinder: gas under pressure. Environment (dead tree and fish).

Product Hazard Degreasers and solvents (acetone, IPA, brake cleaner) Flammable, vapours affect the brain, skin defatting Thread lockers, adhesives Skin sensitisers Epoxy resins and hardeners Sensitisers (dermatitis, asthma) Isocyanate paints (PU), foams Asthma; air-fed mask for spraying Pickling paste (HF/nitric) Severe burns, HF absorbs through skin (calcium gluconate) Caustic soda, acids Burns, eye damage Used oil Skin cancer with long contact, environmental Penetrant and developer sprays Flammable aerosols

Read the SDS before using a new product. Keep SDSs where the crew can find them. Labels on every container, including small decanted bottles. Store flammables in a flammable cabinet; separate acids from caustics and oxidisers from fuels. Spill kits at the work area. Report spills to the environment. Eyewash within 10 seconds' walk of corrosive work.

x: Hearing protection above 85 dB(A) average over 8 h. Every +3 dB doubles the energy: 88 dB allows 4 h, 91 dB 2 h (3 dB exchange rate). If you need to shout to be heard 1 m away, it's over 85 dB. Typical: angle grinder 100–105 dB, air arc gouging 110–120 dB, hydrojetting 110+ dB, steam blowing 130+ dB.

t: Noise, vibration, heat & fatigue › Hand-arm vibration
x: Grinders, impact wrenches, needle guns, chipping hammers. Causes white finger and nerve damage. Limit exposure time (use the tool's m/s² rating and an exposure calculator: EU action value 2.5 m/s² A(8), limit 5 m/s²). Rotate tasks, use low-vibration tools, keep hands warm.

t: Noise, vibration, heat & fatigue › Heat stress
x: Signs of heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, dizziness, nausea, headache, cramps. Move to shade, cool, drink water. Heat stroke: confusion, hot dry skin, collapse. Medical emergency. Cool immediately with water and call for help. Drink about 250 mL every 15–20 minutes in hot work. Don't wait for thirst. Work-rest cycles by WBGT index. Acclimatise new workers over 1–2 weeks. Extra care with chemical suits and inside vessels.

Long shifts (12 h) and night work raise error rates. Limit consecutive shifts and overtime as site rules say. Watch the crew in the last hours of a shift and the early morning hours. Don't schedule critical tasks (lifts, line breaks) at the end of a long shift.

t: Noise, vibration, heat & fatigue › Manual handling
x: Plan the lift. Test the weight. Above 25 kg (male guide, less for women and awkward loads) use help or lifting aids. Feet apart, bend the knees, keep the back straight, hold close, no twisting. Use trolleys, pallet trucks, chain blocks, vacuum lifters.

k: incident report near miss first aid lost time recordable investigation witness statement preserve scene root cause corrective action lessons learned

x: Near miss : could have caused harm but didn't. First aid case , medical treatment case , restricted work , lost time injury , fatality . Property damage, spills, fires, dropped objects, process safety events. Unsafe acts and conditions (observations). The Heinrich/Bird triangle idea: many near misses sit under every serious injury. Fixing near misses prevents the big one.

Make the area safe. Stop work. Care for the injured. First aid, call emergency response. Report to your supervisor and HSE right away. Preserve the scene. Don't move items unless needed for safety. Take photos. Get names of witnesses. Separate them before they discuss it.

Facts first: who, what, where, when. Then how and why. Witness statements in their own words, written soon after. Timeline of events. Root causes (see the RCA topic): 5 Whys, fishbone, or the site's method (TapRooT, ICAM). Corrective actions with owners and dates. Check they work. Share lessons learned with all crews.

x: Stop work, make safe in seconds (close the torch, stop the machine). Go to the muster point by the safe route (check wind direction for gas alarms). Supervisor: headcount against the crew list. Report missing people at once to the muster controller. Stay until released.

Type Good for Not for Water (red) Class A: wood, paper, cloth Electrical, flammable liquids Foam (cream label) A and B (liquids) Live electrical (most types) Dry powder (blue label) A, B, C (gases), electrical Indoors small spaces (visibility) CO₂ (black label) Electrical, B Outdoors in wind, confined spaces (asphyxiation) Wet chemical (yellow) Class F cooking oils PASS: Pull pin, Aim at base of fire, Squeeze, Sweep. Keep your back to an exit. Only fight small fires you can put out quickly.

t: Emergency response › First aid basics (trained first aiders act)
x: Burns: cool with running water for 20 minutes. Don't remove stuck clothing. Cover loosely with cling film. Eye injuries: flush with eyewash for at least 15 minutes (chemicals). Don't rub. Don't remove embedded objects. Bleeding: direct pressure. Unconscious, not breathing: call for help, CPR, AED. High-pressure injection injury (hydraulic, grease gun): looks small but is a surgical emergency.
Stop the source if safe. Contain with absorbent booms and pads. Cover drains. Report to the control room and environment team. Dispose of used absorbents as hazardous waste.

k: safety leadership stop work authority swa safety observation behaviour based safety bbs safety conversation toolbox talk lead by example just culture
x: Stop Work Authority : everyone can stop any job they think is unsafe, without blame. Back them every time, even when they're wrong. Lead by example : wear the PPE, follow the rules, don't take shortcuts when the manager isn't there. Daily toolbox talk : 10 minutes, about today's jobs and hazards, not a generic topic only. Safety conversations : ask open questions at the worksite: "What could hurt you on this job? What would make it safer?" Observations : record safe and unsafe behaviours. Praise good ones publicly, correct unsafe ones privately and immediately. Just culture : honest mistakes a

t: Safety leadership on the floor › Life-saving rules (typical)
x: Work with a valid permit. Verify isolation before work. Obtain authorisation before entering a confined space. Protect yourself against a fall when working at height. Never walk under a suspended load. Obtain authorisation before overriding or disabling safety-critical equipment. Conduct gas tests when required. No alcohol or drugs while working or driving. Follow driving rules (seat belt, no phone, speed).

k: supervisor role responsibilities supervisor skills first line leader accountability crew
x: The supervisor is the link between the plan and the work. Planners, engineers and managers decide what and when. The supervisor makes sure it gets done safely, correctly and on time, with the crew they have.

Safety : permits, JSAs, isolations, PPE, stopping unsafe work. The supervisor is the most important safety person on the job. Quality : work to procedure and specification, measurements recorded, hold points respected. Productivity : crew allocated well, tools and materials ready, delays removed. People : assign, coach, train, discipline fairly, look after welfare. Communication : with operations, planners, QC, other crafts, the client. Records : daily reports, timesheets, job cards, test records.

t: The mechanical supervisor's role › Skills that matter
x: Technical knowledge good enough to spot a wrong method, a bad reading or a missing step. Reading drawings, P IDs, isometrics, manuals and specifications. Planning a day and a week. Clear instructions: what, why, how, by when, and what "done" looks like. Listening and asking questions. Calm under pressure. Problems will come; your reaction sets the tone.

t: The mechanical supervisor's role › First 30 days in a new crew
x: Learn names, skills and certifications of every crew member. Walk the plant with an operator. Learn the units and the bad actors. Read the site's life-saving rules, permit procedure and the main specs. Meet your planner, QC inspector, storeman and operations supervisors. Watch before changing things. Then fix the biggest problem first.

What's stopping you from finishing? The Today page on this site turns this routine into a checklist and builds the shift report for you.

t: Work orders & CMMS › Work order lifecycle
x: Notification / request : someone reports a problem (operator, inspector, supervisor). Approval and priority . Planning : scope, steps, materials, tools, man-hours, permits, drawings. Scheduling : assigned to a date and crew. Execution . Completion : what was found, what was done, parts used, hours, failure codes. Technical close : review by planner/engineer, history updated.

Priority Meaning Response P1 Emergency Safety, environment, or production stopped Immediately P2 Urgent Will fail soon or production reduced Within 24–72 h P3 Normal Planned and scheduled Within 2–4 weeks P4 Low / opportunity When convenient or at shutdown Backlog

t: Work orders & CMMS › A good notification says
x: Equipment tag (P-101B), not "the pump by the tank". Symptom: what is happening (seal leaking 1 drop per second at the DE). When it started, and anything that changed. Effect on production and safety. Photo if possible.

t: Work orders & CMMS › Completing a work order well
x: As found : condition and readings before work. Cause : what you think caused it (failure code). Action : what was done. As left : final readings. Parts : part numbers and quantities used. Follow-up : anything that still needs doing (new notification). "Fixed pump" helps nobody. "Replaced DE mechanical seal (cartridge, type xx). Old seal: heat-checked SiC face, flush orifice 50% blocked with scale. Cleaned orifice, aligned to 0.02/0.01. Recommend strainer in Plan 11 line." builds history that stops the next failure.

t: Job planning & kitting › Job pack contents
x: Work order with clear scope. Job steps (method), with hold points. Drawings, isometrics, OEM manual pages, previous history and readings. JSA, permit requirements, isolation list. Bill of materials with reservation numbers. Special tools and equipment (crane, scaffold, hydraulic tools, lasers). Data sheets for recording measurements. Estimated man-hours and crew make-up.
Walk the job with the planner before scheduling. Check access, scaffold, lifting points, isolation points, laydown area, obstacles, and whether parts on the drawing match what's in the field.

Stores pick all parts and consumables into a tagged kit before the job is scheduled. Supervisor checks the kit the day before: right part numbers, quantities, sizes, materials, certificates. Missing parts are the most common cause of delays and wrench time loss.

t: Job planning & kitting › Scheduling the week
x: Load the crew to about 80–90% of available hours. Leave room for breakdowns. Schedule only "ready" work: planned, materials in hand, permits arranged. Group work by area to reduce travel and permit overhead. Agree the schedule with operations (equipment availability). Measure schedule compliance and discuss why jobs slipped.

x: Scope (12–24 months before): collect work list, challenge each item, freeze scope. Planning : detailed job packs, materials, contractors, scaffolding, cranes, schedules. Pre-turnaround : prefabrication, scaffolding, pre-shutdown inspections, mobilisation. Execution : shutdown, decontamination, isolation, work, inspection, boxing up, testing. Start-up : de-isolation, leak tests, commissioning. Post-turnaround : demobilisation, close-out, lessons learned.

The longest chain of dependent tasks sets the turnaround duration. Typically: big exchangers, column internals, heater, reactor catalyst change, or major compressor overhaul. Put your best crews and supervision on critical path jobs, with 24-hour cover.

Shift handover meetings (face to face). Daily progress meeting: critical path status, emergent work, safety. Emergent work (found during inspection) goes through a quick approve-plan-schedule process. Big emergent jobs can push the critical path.

Know your job packs before the turnaround starts. Check that scaffolds, materials and special tools are in place before the equipment is handed over. Inspection hold points: book inspectors in advance. Keep a blind list and a gasket/bolt record for every joint opened. Box up only after inspection sign-off. Photos of internals before closing. Fatigue: 12-hour shifts for weeks. Watch your crew and yourself.

All blinds removed and checked against the blind list. All joints tagged and torqued, leak tests done. PSVs reinstalled and car-seals in place. Rotating equipment aligned, lubed, coupled, guards on, rotation checked. Housekeeping: scaffolds down, debris removed, drains clear.

k: leadership crew management delegation motivation feedback conflict discipline coaching training apprentices skills matrix

x: Use the five-point brief: What (the task), Why (the purpose), How (key steps, hazards, quality points), Who (who does what), When (deadline and check-in times). Ask them to repeat back the key points.
Match the job to the person's skill. Stretch a little to develop them. Give authority with the responsibility. Check in at agreed points, not constantly.

Praise in public, correct in private. Be specific: "The alignment readings you recorded were clear and complete" beats "good job". For problems: describe the behaviour, the effect, and what you need instead. Listen to their side.
Deal with it early. Talk to each person separately, then together. Focus on the work issue, not personalities. Agree on actions and follow up.
Know the company procedure. Document facts. Be consistent: the same rule for everyone, including your best worker. Safety violations: stop the work immediately, then follow procedure.

Keep a skills matrix: who can do what (alignment, seal change, rigging, welding processes, tests). Pair apprentices with skilled fitters. Rotate them through job types. Use this site's quiz for quick checks before letting someone work alone on a task. Recommend courses and certifications (vibration Cat I/II, rigging, laser alignment, welding inspection).

t: Communication & meetings › Toolbox talks that work
x: 5–10 minutes at the start of the shift. Today's jobs and their main hazards. One lesson from a recent event. Ask questions; let the crew talk. Ask the quiet ones. Record attendance.

Operations own the plant. Ask before touching anything outside your permit scope. Tell them when you start, when you finish, and if anything changes. Report any leak, abnormal noise or condition you see, even if it's not your job.
Escalate early when a job will be late, a safety issue can't be resolved, a quality problem is found, or materials are wrong. Bring the facts and a suggested solution.

Listen before talking. Short, clear messages. Call sign first: "Control, this is Mechanical 2." Use "over" and "out" (or site standard). Repeat back critical instructions. Emergency traffic takes priority.

t: Daily reports & records › Daily report template
x: Date, shift, area, supervisor. Manpower by trade and hours. Equipment on site. Work completed (by work order or job number). Work in progress and % complete. Problems, delays and their causes (waiting permits, materials, weather). Safety: incidents, near misses, observations, toolbox talk topic. Quality: inspections done, NCRs. Plan for next shift.

Facts and numbers: "3 of 8 flanges torqued" not "flanges progressing". Delays with duration and cause: "Waited 2 h for gas test (tester at another job)." Keep it short. One page. The Today page builds a shift report from your checklist and notes and copies it for email or messaging.

x: Request materials early, with exact part numbers and specs. Check the BOM against the field. Inspect on receipt: right item, quantity, damage, certificates, heat numbers. Keep traceability on site: tag, store off the ground, segregate stainless and alloys. Control consumables: welding rods, discs, gaskets, studs. Issue against jobs. Return surplus to stores, tagged. Scrap in the right bins (metal, hazardous waste).

t: Materials, stores & cost control › Cost drivers a supervisor controls
x: Rework : the most expensive hour is the second time you do the job. Get it right first time. Waiting time : permits, materials, cranes. Plan ahead. Overtime : plan it; use it for critical work, not to cover poor planning. Equipment rental : off-hire cranes, scaffolds and compressors as soon as they're done. Consumables waste : wet rods, discs used past half life, gaskets dropped and scrapped.

x: Onboarding: site induction, competence checks (certificates, welder tickets, rigging cards), introduction to permit and LOTO rules. Clear written scope. Changes go through a variation process, not a verbal "while you're there". Agree who supplies what: tools, consumables, scaffolds, cranes, PPE. Same safety rules for everyone. Stop unsafe work, report it to the contractor supervisor and HSE. Quality: same ITP, same hold points. Check their records. Daily coordination meeting for interfaces (who's in which area, which permits). Review performance at the end: safety, quality, schedule, cooperati

DWG PHD-08 · ইন্সপেকশন ইন্সপেকশন চেকলিস্ট ও পদ্ধতি রাউন্ডে চলমান অবস্থায় যা দেখবেন, শাটডাউনে ভেতরে ঢুকে যা দেখবেন, কোন যন্ত্রে মাপবেন, আর কোন মানে সতর্ক হবেন। চেকলিস্টে টিক দিলে এই ডিভাইসে মনে থাকে। চেকলিস্ট — পদ্ধতি ১২টি NDT/CM সংরক্ষণ এই ডিভাইসে প্রিন্ট হ্যাঁ 08.1 ইন্টারঅ্যাকটিভ চেকলিস্ট গ্রানুলেটর ড্রায়ার কোটিং ড্রাম দৈনিক রাউন্ড (চলন্ত) সাপ্তাহিক/মাসিক শাটডাউন (ভেতর) ০ / ০ ০% এই তালিকা মুছুন প্রিন্ট করুন 08.2 ইন্সপেকশন ও কন্ডিশন মনিটরিং পদ্ধতি পদ্ধতি কোথায় যন্ত্র কী ধরা পড়ে কতবার দৃশ্যমান (Visual) সব জায়গা টর্চ, আয়না, ক্যামেরা, স্ট্রোবোস্কোপ লিক, ফাটল, ক্ষয়, ঢিলা বোল্ট, স্প্রে প্যাটার্ন প্রতি শিফট তাপমাত্রা (স্পট) বেয়ারিং, গিয়ারবক্স, শেল IR থার্মোমিটার অস্বাভাবিক গরম প্রতি শিফট
